Revision 60's contract was then implemented verbatim and attacked. Every row
below is an executed result, not a reading:

| unreviewed commit at `HEAD`, worktree clean and equal to it | revision 60 | revision 61 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| rogue writer added **and** conformance rebound to always-`PASS` | `PASS` | `VERIFIER_UNAPPROVED` |

| excluded/metadata-only commit after approval | `PASS` | `PASS` (no false staleness) |
| fresh technical approval of the exact changed content | — | `PASS` (eligible again) |

The fourth row is worth stating plainly: revision 60 *does* answer `FAIL` when
only the subject regresses, because the honest conformance still runs. The
defect is not that revision 60 always passes; it is that revision 60 lets the
**checker** be replaced in the same unreviewed commit as the **checked**, and
then believes it.

**Correction applied**, along all six of the finding's required lines, and
deliberately reusing the existing machinery rather than adding a second one.
`D-Completion-Obligations` now separates **subject identity** `(C,
obligation_content_id)` from **verifier identity** `(verifier_identity_id,
verifier_census)`; requires `approval_is_current(..., stage="implementation",
head=C)` on the obligation's **owning** work item before any `PASS` is
load-bearing; takes the approved verifier blobs from that record's
`review_content_manifest`; proves the verifier content at `C` equals them; and
**materializes and executes the verifier from the approved blobs** — the same
`git cat-file`-into-scratch mechanism revision 60 already used for the
serialization helper, now applied to the checker. Two fail-closed
classifications are added, `VERIFIER_UNAPPROVED` and `VERIFIER_UNRESOLVABLE`.

This works because the implementation-stage projection hashes protected
*content* and never folds the commit id in, so the predicate says exactly the
right thing: byte-identical protected content is current, an unreviewed
protected change is not, and an excluded/metadata commit is neither. That last
property is the finding's own "excluded or provenance-permitted metadata commits
must not create false technical-approval staleness" requirement, and it is
satisfied by the existing rules rather than by a carve-out.

`derive_obligation_verdict(repo_root, obligation_id, C)` a pure function of
`(obligation_id, C)`. It is not: `C` pins the subject, not the checker. The
plan now states the true function as
`derive_obligation_verdict(obligation_id, subject_identity, verifier_identity)`,
records the verifier identity and its approval provenance in
`completion_obligations_accepted`, and defines replay as *materialize the
recorded verifier blobs and execute them*, never *call today's function with the
recorded commit*. Verified both ways: after the live verifier was rebound to
always-`PASS` and its derivation entry point renamed out of existence, replay
from the recorded identity stayed bit-for-bit identical, and an unreachable
recorded blob classified `REPLAY_UNRESOLVABLE` instead of falling back to live.

**What is not claimed.** This is a review-authority boundary, not a
cryptographic one, and `D-Completion-Obligations` now says so in as many words —
a process already running unreviewed code can decline to perform any check, and
no design executed by the thing it distrusts can prevent that. This plan has
twice been caught overclaiming in exactly this place (revision 59 about digests,
revision 60 about replay), so the boundary is stated rather than papered over.

**Revision 60's protections are untouched**: immutable Git-object subject reads,

Three passes from three deliberately different perspectives, executed against

   requires *that* item to hold a technical approval.

The passes also confirmed the properties the round was asked to prove and found

moment an unreviewed serialization change appears.

real repository fact, and is recorded as an implementation obligation rather

## WF8b finding disposition (revision 59 → 60) — external plan review confirmed `GPT-R76-*` resolved but found the new completion-obligation evidence record self-asserted, its freshness projection blind to writer-set membership, and its verdict unprotected between evaluation and terminal publication (`GPT-R77-001`/`-002`/`-003`)

External plan review of revision 59 returned `Status: REVISE`, **zero blocking
findings and three important findings**. The reviewer independently reproduced
`bundle_id` `b592fa7d…`, rebuilt the plan-stage projection from first
principles to `review_content_id` `b0023327…`, confirmed the 63-row
normalization zero-mismatch, reran all 489 hermetic tests green, and
independently re-derived the twelve-writer inventory from the live
`.claude/commands/` directory. `GPT-R76-001` and `-002` were closed outright;
`GPT-R76-003` was closed at the registry/completion-ownership level, with the
new evidence mechanism itself carrying the three residual findings. **The
approval transaction was not reopened, and this revision does not reopen it.**

All three findings share one boundary and one question, and the user's
instruction for this round was explicit that they are not three independent
metadata patches: the workflow needs one trustworthy, complete, freshness-bound
and stable answer to *"has `WFO-STATE-SERIALIZATION` actually passed for the
exact implementation and complete writer set being accepted?"*, and that one
answer must be authoritative for both quiescence retirement and WF8b/work-item
completion. This revision's correction is therefore a single structural change
rather than three: **the gate derives the verdict by running the conformance
itself, against an immutable Git commit, over a dynamically discovered writer
set.** Removing the record removes all three attack surfaces at once, and the
result is a smaller mechanism than revision 59's, not a larger one.

Each finding was reproduced mechanically against this repository before being
accepted; none was taken on the finding's own framing.

### `GPT-R77-001` — important — a `CURRENT_PASS` was self-asserted

Accepted in full, and reproduced first. Revision 59's projection
(`sha256` over the Git blob identities of the twelve writer command files, the
serialization helper and the conformance test, plus the obligation id) and its
four-state classification rule were implemented verbatim in an isolated
harness and run against this repository's live content. Results:

| attack | revision 59's verdict |
| --- | --- |
| hand-written `status: "PASS"` + exact live digest, arbitrary `produced_by` | `CURRENT_PASS` |
| same, with `produced_by` copied from a legitimate-looking run | `CURRENT_PASS` |
| an existing `FAILED` entry edited to `PASS`, nothing rerun | `CURRENT_PASS` |

The reviewer's conclusion is exactly right and worth restating plainly: the
digest is *intended* to be recomputable by the verifier, which makes it equally
precomputable by whoever writes the file. A content digest can attest to
content; it cannot attest to a test result. Revision 59's sentence "nothing
else may produce that record; a hand-written or hand-edited one fails its own
digest check" was mechanically false, and this revision says so rather than
softening it. The artifact was also deliberately excluded from both plan- and
implementation-stage review identity, so fabricating it staled no approval —
which made the defect load-bearing rather than theoretical.

**Correction applied: `GPT-R77-001`'s own preferred option (1).** The gate runs
the conformance and derives `PASS`/`FAIL` from that execution. No record is
written, so option (3)'s "a hand-written record with the correct digest but no
verified execution must classify as untrusted" is satisfied in the strongest
available form — there is no record to classify. Option (2)'s attestation model
was considered and rejected on the reviewer's own terms: a genuine attestation
needs a real trusted authority and a way for the verifier to prove provenance,
this repository has no signing boundary, and an unsigned local JSON file with
more fields is the very thing the finding rules out.
`docs/ai-workflow/registry/<work_item_id>-completion-evidence.json` is not
created; a file of that name is never read, and is proven to contribute nothing
to any verdict or identity whether it is absent, present, says `PASS`, or says
`FAILED` (item 356(c)).

### `GPT-R77-002` — important — freshness bound twelve remembered paths, not the discovered writer set

Accepted in full, and reproduced: with revision 59's fixed-membership
projection, adding a thirteenth installed command that writes
`WORKFLOW_STATE.json` without taking the lock left the recomputed
`obligation_content_id` **bit-for-bit identical** and the prior evidence
`CURRENT_PASS`, while a live discovery over the same directory returned
thirteen writers against a projection still binding twelve. The reviewer's
diagnosis of why is precise: the gate recomputed a digest but never re-ran the
discovery whose *runtime result* is what the invariant depends on.

**Correction applied**, along all five of the finding's required lines, and
collapsed into `GPT-R77-001`'s fix exactly as the finding anticipates:

1. one authoritative implementation, `discover_state_writers(repo_root, C)`,
   whose return value **is** both the set the conformance validates and the
   projection the identity binds — the same object, not two computations
   asserted to agree (item 357(a)/(b));
2. the identity binds an ordered `{path, blob}` census, never a count or a
   prose list;
3. supported surfaces are widened beyond `.claude/commands/` to every declared
   writer surface, and the surface definitions are themselves part of the
   projection, so narrowing them is a content change;
4. adding, removing, renaming or rewriting a writer recomputes the verdict —
   trivially, because nothing is cached;
5. the two-inventory hazard that produced the 8-vs-12 drift is structurally
   impossible, and item 357(a) asserts no second inventory and no literal

Twelve survives as a **recorded observation of today's repository** (item
357(c)), which is the reviewer's acceptance criterion 13, and the prototype
reproduces it: live discovery against the converted-repository model returns

### `GPT-R77-003` — important — the state-file lock protected neither the evidence nor the content the verdict depended on

Accepted in full, and reproduced with real processes in three shapes. In each,
the completing process held `WORKFLOW_STATE.lock` across
evaluate-gate-then-publish exactly as revision 59 specified, while a second
process mutated something the verdict depended on:

| racer's action while the state lock was held | outcome |
| --- | --- |
| evidence `PASS → FAILED` | `MILESTONE_COMPLETE` published, final evidence `FAILED` |
| evidence deleted | `MILESTONE_COMPLETE` published, evidence absent |
| a writer's content rewritten | `MILESTONE_COMPLETE` published from a now-stale verdict |

The lock serialized state writers correctly throughout; it simply had no
relationship to the files being mutated. **Revision 59's item 356(i) claim is
withdrawn**, and this plan now asserts nowhere that `WORKFLOW_STATE.lock`
protects a file it does not lock — the finding's required correction (5).

**Correction applied: the finding's required correction (1), the immutable
reviewed-content source**, and deliberately *not* the "re-read immediately
before publish" the finding rules out. The gate pins one commit `C` and reads
every input the verdict depends on — including the serialization helper's own
source, which the behavioural sub-suite materializes out of `C` and executes
there — from Git objects, never from the working tree. The derivation is a pure
function of `(obligation_id, C)`, so there is no interval in which it can
change and therefore no window to close. Required correction (2) is met
vacuously: no mutable evidence remains part of the authority. Required
correction (3) is met by `completion_obligations_accepted`, written into the
work item entry by `complete_work_item(...)` and published in the same bytes as
`MILESTONE_COMPLETE`, recording verdict, `source_commit`,
`obligation_content_id` and writer count — replayable exactly, including after
later history lands (item 356(l)/(m)). Required correction (4) is met by
quiescence retirement calling the identical function under identical pinning.
(**This paragraph's original closing clause — "the bridge carries its pinned
`C` in `quiescence_authorization` and passes it back as `expected_commit`,
which asserts rather than redirects" — is superseded and withdrawn by revision
61, `GPT-R78-002`**: it contradicted the schema-version-3 journal, in which
`quiescence_authorization` is the literal user text, and it was
self-invalidating across the transaction's own step-6 approval commit. The
shared identical-call rule stands unchanged; the consumer that performs the
retirement is item 347's permanent `/approve-review`, never the temporary
bridge. See "WF8b finding disposition (revision 60 → 61)".)

The single-critical-section ordering revision 59 introduced is *kept* — the
registry read and the state read must still not straddle the publish — but it
is no longer load-bearing for verdict stability, and the plan now says which
job it does. Lock ordering is unchanged (guard first, then `flock`), and the
conformance is proven to acquire neither, so no inversion is introduced: the
whole gate is exercised with the live lock actually held and completes without
deadlock, with the lock still held by the caller afterwards (item 356(n)).

### Bounded adversarial stress passes

Three passes from three deliberately different perspectives, each executed
against isolated scratch repositories and real processes rather than read for
plausibility. Five further concrete defects were found in this same mechanism,
all validated, all fixed, and all re-verified with the earlier passes re-run as
regressions. The repair-cycle bound was reached with nothing outstanding.

**Pass 1 — forgery and freshness.** Replayed every revision-59 attack against
the new design and swept the writer-set add/remove/rename/change matrix. Two
defects:

1. *the identity bound only the declared-writer subset*. An **undeclared**
   thirteenth file added to a writer surface correctly produced `FAIL` but left
   `obligation_content_id` unchanged, so two materially different repositories
   shared an identity — harmless while nothing caches by identity, but the
   identity is exactly what the terminal transition records as its audit
   binding. Fixed by binding the **complete surface census** rather than the
   writer subset.
2. *the authoritative derivation could not be distinguished from the
   worktree-sensitive resolution*. Fixed by factoring the two apart:
   `derive_obligation_verdict(...)` reads only Git objects and is pure;
   `resolve_obligation(...)` pins, applies the divergence precondition, and
   delegates. The precondition can now only ever refuse, which is what makes
   "the working tree cannot change a derived verdict" a testable statement
   rather than a hope.

**Pass 2 — trust boundaries, discovery completeness, determinism.** Two
defects:

3. *a caller-supplied commit was a caller-supplied verdict* — the
   `GPT-R37-001` shape this plan has already removed twice. With `HEAD`
   genuinely failing, handing the gate an ancestor commit at which the
   conformance passed, and restoring the working tree to that ancestor's
   content so the divergence precondition stayed silent, returned `PASS`.
   Fixed by removing the parameter: the gate resolves `HEAD` itself, and a
   caller's pin becomes an `expected_commit` assertion that refuses
   (`PIN_MOVED`).
4. *namespaced commands were undiscovered*. Claude Code installs commands as
   `.claude/commands/<ns>/<name>.md`; a one-directory-level surface rule left
   an unlocked namespaced writer entirely invisible and the gate returned
   `PASS`. Fixed by making surfaces recursive.

**Pass 3 — Git object resolution, conformance determinism, audit binding.**
One defect and one hardening:

5. *the behavioural conformance discriminated by luck*. A publisher that reads
   outside the critical section was rejected only because sixteen racing
   processes happened to interleave badly. A gate whose refusal depends on
   winning a race is not a gate. Fixed by leading with a **deterministic
   barrier-based interleaving test** — a harness holds the lock, lets the
   writer start, publishes a value, releases; a correct publisher preserves
   that value, an incorrect one necessarily clobbers it — with the N-way
   concurrency test retained as an additional check, not the discriminator.
   Verified: 0/5 false passes on the broken publisher, deterministically, where
   the previous test was probabilistic.
6. *`git replace` refs rewrite what an object id resolves to*, which would
   break exactly the content-addressing the design rests on. Hardened: every
   Git read uses `--no-replace-objects` with `GIT_NO_REPLACE_OBJECTS=1`.
   Exercised in both directions, including the dangerous one — substituting
   honest bytes over a failing blob is confirmed unable to launder that
   identity into a `PASS`.

Pass 3 also probed three discovery-surface escapes. Two were real and are
fixed by making surfaces extension-agnostic (`rogue.bash`,
`rogue.markdown` both escaped an extension-keyed rule and both now refuse).
The third — hiding a writer as `scripts/*_test.py`, the one deliberate surface
exclusion — was examined and **not** classified as a defect: the exclusion
exists so that unrelated test edits do not manufacture false staleness, and the
exploit path is closed elsewhere, since any command delegating its state write
to such a module fails the routing check. That is asserted directly rather than
argued (item 357(i)).

### What this revision deliberately does not touch

The user's instruction for this round was to keep the approval/bootstrap
transaction stable unless validation proved otherwise, and validation did not.
Revision 59's non-breakable classification for delayed durable operations, the
transaction mutation/handoff guard, the fully-written no-replace journal
publication, the explicit approval owner/takeover model, the index-pinned
approval state, the exact expected-post-state binding, the exact committed
state bytes, the exact committed path set, the exact declaration bytes, the
exhaustive post-amend verification, the temporary state-writer quiescence
window, the process-scoped `fcntl.flock` serialization primitive, item 354's
ownership by reachable `WF8b` continued scope, and the rule that completion and
quiescence consume the same obligation all survive unchanged. The twelve-writer
current inventory survives as a verified observation rather than as a
mechanism input. No finding was rejected, and no unrelated cleanup was folded
in.

## WF8b finding disposition (revision 58 → 59) — external plan review confirmed `GPT-R75-*` resolved but found the authorized guard break unsafe for post-durability mutations, the permanent state lock's takeover semantics unsound, and item 354's completion dependency unrepresented in any helper (`GPT-R76-001`/`-002`/`-003`)

External plan review of revision 58 returned `Status: REVISE`, **zero blocking
findings and three important findings**. The reviewer independently reproduced
`bundle_id` `2e2dfb99…`, rebuilt the plan-stage projection to
`review_content_id` `6a6215b6…`, confirmed the 63-row normalization
zero-mismatch, and reran all 489 hermetic tests green. `GPT-R75-001` was closed
for ordinary, non-forced ownership transfer; `GPT-R75-002` for the temporary
bridge's stated safe-execution contract; `GPT-R75-003` for basic reachability.

All three new findings were **validated against this repository before
acceptance** and all three were accepted. None was rejected.

### `GPT-R76-001` — important — the authorized guard break is unsafe for post-durability mutations

Accepted in full, and reproduced in both halves the finding names, then
reproduced again against the fix.

Revision 58's residual argument was that every breakable operation is "detected
or harmless." The reviewer's insight is that revision 58 checked for the
existence of a downstream check without asking whether that check **still runs
when the operation actually lands**. For step 8b the answer is decisive, and in
a way that is worth stating precisely because it is counter-intuitive: journal
close does not merely end the transaction, it **ends the quiescence window**,
and therefore *legalizes* exactly the foreign state writes a delayed
materialization would overwrite. The two are the same event.

Reproduced, with the ordering the round's brief specifies:

```
T acquires 8b guard + assert_owner OK, paused before os.replace
takeover: acquired via authorized break
takeover: rotated T -> T2, released guard
T2: completed 8b, closed journal — quiescence window ENDS
foreign: legal post-quiescence write, other.state_revision=8
T (displaced): delayed os.replace lands, other.state_revision=7
```

and for the amend:

```
T acquires 7(d) guard + assert_owner OK, amend staged and paused
takeover: acquired via authorized break
T2: verified HEAD=aa9f074d, closed journal
T (displaced): delayed amend lands, HEAD=3fbf3571
```

`HEAD` was rewritten away from the commit the replacement owner had verified,
after the journal was gone, with hooks re-running.

**The fix is a rule, not a patch list.** Step classification is now decided by
the latest point at which a delayed completion can still affect durable state:
a mutation is `"destructive"` — never breakable — if its already-issued
completion could still be externally visible after a replacement owner has
completed every downstream check *and closed the journal*; it is `"ordinary"`
only if its late completion is mechanically detected before the transaction can
close, or genuinely harmless in **every** state reachable after journal close.
Applying it:

- `step-8b-materialize` → `"destructive"` (required explicitly);
- `step-7d-amend-commit` → `"destructive"` (required explicitly);
- `step-6.5-commit` → `"destructive"` (**this revision's own extension** under
  required correction (3): revision 58 leaned on the outcome classifier, but
  the classifier is the *new owner's* step, and a delayed `git commit` landing
  after close creates a second commit carrying the same
  `Workflow-Plan-Approval` trailer with no transaction left to resolve the
  resulting ambiguity);
- the rollback's index reset and both journal deletions remain
  `"destructive"`, unchanged and unweakened;
- **only index-only staging** remains `"ordinary"`.

Re-running both reproductions against the new classification: the takeover is
refused in both, the journal still carries `T`, and `HEAD` is unchanged.

**The "harmless after close" clause is discharged, not asserted.** Revision 58's
claim that index staging is "caught before any commit" was too strong, exactly
as the finding says. The residual table now gives each remaining case its
*latest* detection point — 6.3/6.4, then step 7's three committed-content
checks, then step 8's manifest recomputation for protected paths, then step 9's
clean-tree confirmation — and, past journal close, the honest answer: the
approval commit is durable and unalterable by an index entry, so the residue is
a dirty index that the **next** run refuses on at step 3. Verified against real
Git for all four remaining `"ordinary"` guards, each with its operation delayed
until after journal close and after a legal foreign state write: `HEAD`
unmoved, approval commit intact, state file unchanged, foreign update intact,
residue exactly one staged path, and the index-isolation precondition refusing.

**One cost is accepted and stated.** A session abandoned inside a destructive
window has no in-band resolution. The documented alternative is an out-of-band
manual guard clearance in which the user establishes that the holding session
is genuinely gone and removes the guard by hand — categorically different from
an in-band break, because the user is asserting a fact about process liveness
they can actually verify rather than the procedure inferring it. Nothing is
lost by the wait: the journal, its bound pre/post state, and the durable Git
record are all intact, and the next session's step 0 completes forward or rolls
back exactly as it would have.

### `GPT-R76-002` — important — the permanent state lock copied takeover semantics into a context that cannot support them

Accepted in full. Reproduced exactly as described, with the generic
state-writer ordering:

```
A: acquired persistent lock, read {'a': 0, 'b': 0}
takeover: persistent lock rotated to B (A is actually still alive)
B: read {'a': 0, 'b': 0}, published {'a': 0, 'b': 1}
A (displaced): resumed and published stale {'a': 1, 'b': 0}
final: {'a': 1, 'b': 0}   ← B's update lost
```

The diagnosis the finding offers is the right one and this revision adopts it
verbatim: the approval bootstrap needed durable ownership because it spans
**separate short-lived processes**; an ordinary state write does not, and
copying the takeover model there imported a takeover with none of the machinery
that made it safe.

**The primitive becomes a process-scoped `fcntl.flock`**, held across the
complete read → mutate → canonical-serialize → atomic-publish critical section,
with **no takeover, no owner token, and no user authorization**. Verified with
real processes:

- a paused holder blocks a second writer for exactly its hold (1.2 s), after
  which both updates are present;
- a writer killed mid-section (`os._exit` while holding) releases immediately —
  the next writer proceeded with no manual break, and the dead writer's partial
  update was simply absent;
- sixteen concurrent writers preserved every update;
- a second `os.open` + `flock(LOCK_EX)` in the *same* process would block
  (`LOCK_EX | LOCK_NB` raises `BlockingIOError`), so nested state writes are
  **explicitly refused** rather than nested-acquired;
- the lock file carries no ownership at rest and is immediately acquirable once
  the holder exits.

Two further requirements from the finding are met explicitly. **The read that
feeds the write is inside the critical section** — every installed command
reads state early for preflight purposes and then works for a long time before
persisting, so the contract names the persist-time re-read as the authoritative
one and forbids the "lock only around the final write" shape by name. This is a
re-ordering rather than a redesign: all fifteen state transitions in
`workflow_state.py` are already pure `state -> new_state` functions, verified by
inspection. And **all twelve installed writers were re-inspected individually**,
not from a remembered inventory.

### `GPT-R76-003` — important — item 354's completion dependency existed only in prose

Accepted in full, and re-confirmed against the bundled helpers rather than the
finding's text:

```
live work item                      : registry_completion_status(...) == (False, 'WF8b')
same item, only WF8b.status=COMPLETE: registry_completion_status(...) == (True, None)
                                      select_next_checkpoint(...)     == None
workflow_state.py mentions "354"    : False
```

No item-354 fact exists for those helpers to consume, so revision 58's
conformance proved only "`WF8b` is currently incomplete."

The fix is a new normative section, **`D-Completion-Obligations`**, defined once
as a reusable mechanism rather than as a special case for item 354:

> **Superseded in part, revision 60 (`GPT-R77-001`/`-002`/`-003`).** The
> registry declaration, the single terminal predicate, the
> `complete_work_item`-only terminal writer, and the shared
> completion/quiescence consumer all survive unchanged. The **evidence
> artifact and its `CURRENT_PASS`/`STALE` classification do not**: a
> hand-written record carrying the exact live digest was reproduced
> classifying `CURRENT_PASS`, a thirteenth writer was reproduced leaving that
> digest unchanged, and the state-file lock was reproduced protecting neither
> the record nor the content. Revision 60 replaces the record with a verdict
> the gate *derives* by executing the conformance against an immutable pinned
> commit and a live-discovered writer set. The bullets below record what
> revision 59 built; `D-Completion-Obligations` itself is authoritative.

- a registry checkpoint may declare `completion_obligations: ["WFO-…"]`;
  `WF8b` declares `WFO-STATE-SERIALIZATION`. Because the registry is a
  protected plan-stage path, declaring or removing one requires a fresh plan
  approval;
- evidence lives in
  `docs/ai-workflow/registry/<work_item_id>-completion-evidence.json`, under a
  prefix already plan-stage *and* implementation-stage excluded (verified by
  running both classifiers on the path), so recording evidence stales no
  approval;
- freshness is a **content binding**: `obligation_content_id` digests the twelve
  writer command files, the serialization helper and the conformance test. A
  `PASS` recorded before any of them changes is stale by construction. Verified
  both ways: re-timestamping a `PASS` left it `CURRENT_PASS`; substituting a
  single changed writer blob made it `STALE`;
- three helpers resolve it, and **`work_item_completion_status(...)`** is the
  single terminal predicate: terminal iff registry-terminal **and** every
  obligation `CURRENT_PASS`;
- `complete_work_item` — verified to be the **only** function in the bundled
  implementation that writes `phase = "MILESTONE_COMPLETE"` — consumes it and
  raises `UnsatisfiedCompletionObligationError` otherwise;
- **quiescence retirement consumes the identical call**, so the two cannot
  disagree.

`select_next_checkpoint`/`registry_completion_status` deliberately keep their
registry-only semantics, because `scoped_remediation_gate_reachable` and
`milestone_complete_gate_reachable` split on exactly that predicate and
continued-scope remediation is the correct path while an obligation is
outstanding. The finding's required correction (3) is satisfied by its other
permitted route: the higher-level gate rejects the terminal registry result.

Exercised against the real registry and state with **every** checkpoint forced
`COMPLETE`:

| evidence | registry says terminal | completion gate | quiescence retired | agree |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| absent | yes | **refused** | no | yes |
| failed | yes | **refused** | no | yes |
| stale | yes | **refused** | no | yes |
| current pass | yes | allowed | yes | yes |

A second, synthetic obligation declared on a different checkpoint was enforced
by the same code path with no new special case.

### Scope

Nothing outside this system was changed. Revision 58's mutation/handoff guard
remains the ordinary ownership-transfer primitive, its non-nesting rule intact;
the twelve-writer enumeration and item 354's `WF8b` ownership are unchanged;
journal publication, explicit takeover, exact post-state binding, index-pinned
state, exact committed-content checks and the exhaustive three-check post-amend
verification all survive intact. The temporary quiescence window remains
mandatory and is now retired only against a machine-readable fact. No
`WORKFLOW_STATE.json` schema change: the obligation declaration lives in the
registry and the evidence in a separate artifact, so `workflow-v2-1-core`
remains compatible with `governing_workflow_version: "1"` throughout. No new
`WFR` row and no `WFR` description change — `WFR-63`'s acceptance/test column
carries this round — so the 63-row plan/mapping normalization stays
zero-mismatch.

## Stress-pass findings (revision 62)

Three passes from three deliberately different perspectives, each re-run in full
as a regression after every repair. The bounded rule's cycle limit (three
repair/stress cycles) is what ends the loop. Every pass was **executed** —
isolated scratch Git repositories, real commits, real Git object reads, real
interpreter subprocesses — not read for plausibility. **53 executable checks
are green** as of revision 62: 19 reproducing `GPT-R79-001`'s ten required cases,
11 reproducing `GPT-R79-002`'s closure/replay cases, and 8 + 10 + 5 across the
three passes.

The harness for passes 1 and 3 builds a realistic scratch **clone** of this
repository with item 359's classification gap closed *in the clone only*, records
a genuine durable technical-approval commit, and drives every identity through
this repository's own `scripts/workflow_fingerprint.py` rather than a
re-implementation of it. Pass 2's harness builds minimal purpose-built
repositories instead, because its subject is import mechanics rather than
approval mechanics, and every isolation probe runs in a **fresh interpreter
process** that asserts from inside itself that no loaded module resolves to the
live repository.

**Pass 1 — durable approval authority.** Attacked fabricated live approvals,
copied digest/manifest/commit metadata, missing and unreachable approval commits,
ambiguous approval commits, live/durable divergence, stale approvals, allowed
excluded commits, unreviewed verifier/fingerprint-helper/writer changes, a
rewritten live `base_commit`, a flipped `work_item_type`, a malformed committed
state file, and an approval trailer attributed to another work item. 8/8, no
repair required. The notable **negative** result is that the live
`<work_item_id>-artifacts.json` cannot be used to launder an unreviewed change
out of the recomputed identity: the implementation-stage projection folds the
four classification sets into the hashed projection directly, so editing the
declaration changes the digest rather than the classification outcome. That is an
existing property of the shipped implementation, verified here rather than added,
and it is the reason no fix was needed for the one live/pinned split this
mechanism still contains.

**Pass 2 — verifier execution closure.** Attacked a missing
`workflow_fingerprint.py`, live-module fallback, a new repository-local verifier
import, a dependency changed without approval, dependencies deleted and renamed
in later history, subject/verifier identity confusion, historical replay after
arbitrary later repository changes, `git replace` refs, `PYTHONPATH`
contamination, and cached modules leaking in from the live repository. 10/10
after one generalization: the first draft's flat module map could not see a
**package** dependency, which failed closed at execution but left the census
silently under-covering. Generalized so a package name maps to its `__init__.py`
and contributes its whole tracked subtree, with materialization preserving
layout. Re-verified in both directions, and the live closure re-derived
afterwards is unchanged at the same two files.

**Pass 3 — the integration seam, from the false-refusal direction.** This pass
deliberately inverted the question: instead of "can an attacker get a `PASS`",
it asked "can a legitimate repository be refused forever". That found the round's
one substantive defect.

1. **`R62-S3-001` — the census rule refused legitimate repositories forever.**
   The draft required every derived verifier dependency to appear in the durable
   `review_content_manifest`. That manifest covers only paths **changed** in
   `base..commit`, so a dependency untouched since `base_commit` is legitimately
   absent from it. Reproduced in a minimal faithful repository where the
   fingerprint helper was committed at `base` and never changed: the derived
   closure contained it, the approved manifest did not, and the draft refused
   permanently. This is revision 61's own `R61-S3-001` shape — a fail-closed
   rule producing a **false** refusal that makes the obligation uncompletable —
   reappearing at the new binding, which is exactly why the pass was aimed here.
   Fixed: manifest-covered paths bind their approved blob; uncovered paths must
   be **proven** byte-identical at `C` and at `base_commit`, with each census
   entry recording which source bound it. Verified in both directions — the
   legitimate case authorizes, and a later change to that same dependency stales
   the approval and brings the path back into the recomputed manifest.
2. **`R62-S3-002` — `base_commit` was still a live, mutable authority input.**
   It is folded into the projection, but the draft read it from live state while
   reading everything else from the durable side. Rewriting it was confirmed not
   to authorize anything, so this was a completeness defect rather than an
   exploit — but leaving one authority-bearing digest input outside the durable
   record's reach is precisely what this boundary exists to close. Fixed: the
   live `base_commit` must equal the one the approval commit committed.

The pass also confirmed the item-359 condition honestly: run against the **live**
repository, the revision-62 authority chain classifies `VERIFIER_UNRESOLVABLE`
rather than crashing or passing, which is the answer this plan claims and not a
more convenient one.

## Stress-pass findings (revision 61)

Three passes, three repairs, each pass re-run in full as a regression after
every repair. The bounded rule's cycle limit (three repair/stress cycles) is
what ends the loop. Every pass was **executed** — isolated scratch Git
repositories, real commits, real Git object reads — not read for plausibility;
**84 executable checks are green across the three passes** as of revision 61.

The harness builds a scratch repository in the *converted* post-item-354 state
(twelve declared writers routing through one publisher, one declared non-writer,
a verifier module holding discovery, the obligation-to-conformance binding, the
projection and the derivation), implements revision 60's contract verbatim, and
then layers revision 61's verifier authority on top. Crucially, the
implementation-stage `review_content_id` and `review_content_manifest` in every
check are computed by this repository's **own**
`scripts/workflow_fingerprint.py`, so what is validated is the authority binding
the workflow actually ships, not a model of it.

### Pass 1 — "can an unreviewed implementation authorize itself?" (`R61-S1-001`, fixed)

Replayed `GPT-R78-001`'s attack surface end to end: an unreviewed verifier
rebound to unconditional `PASS`; the binding changed alone; discovery changed to
omit a broken writer; a subject-only regression; a worktree deliberately clean
and equal to the unreviewed `HEAD`; excluded-only commits after approval; a
fresh approval of the exact changed content; and historical replay after the
live verifier was changed. Revision 60 returned `PASS` on three of the attacks;
revision 61 refuses all of them and keeps the legitimate paths eligible. 25
checks.

**`R61-S1-001`** — *the verifier identity was not a verifier identity*. The
first draft hashed `{verifier_path_set, verifier_census,
approved_review_content_id}`. Executing "change a writer, re-approve, compare"
showed `verifier_identity_id` rotating even though the verifier's own blob was
byte-identical: the approval digest covers **all** protected implementation
content, so folding it in re-merged subject and verifier identity — exactly what
`GPT-R78-001` asks to separate — and would have made a stable historical
verifier identity impossible. Fixed by hashing `{verifier_path_set,
verifier_census}` only and recording the approval provenance
(`technical_approval_commit`, `approved_review_content_id`) alongside rather
than inside it. Re-verified: a subject-only change now leaves
`verifier_identity_id` byte-identical.

### Pass 2 — "provenance edges and the exact pre/post-approval lifecycle" (`R61-S2-001`, fixed)

A deliberately different perspective: not "can the checker be swapped" but "what
happens at the ragged edges of the authority record, and across the commit the
approval procedure itself creates". 32 checks, covering every incomplete
authority shape, the unclassified-path condition, the permanent/temporary
lifecycle split, and fourteen separate authorization-refusal cases for the
bridge.

**`R61-S2-001`** — *the permanent command would stale its own authority with its
own required commit*. When the conditional fifth member applies, the
`Workflow-Plan-Approval` commit rewrites
`docs/ai-workflow/registry/workflow-v2-1-core-artifacts.json`, which is
implementation-stage protected **by exact path**. Re-resolving approval currency
after that commit therefore refuses — `GPT-R78-002`(C)'s self-invalidating shape
reappearing at the new binding, one revision later, which is precisely why the
pass looked for it. Fixed by defining the permanent command's pin as the derived
`(obligation_content_id, verifier_identity_id)` rather than as a `HEAD` SHA or a
second currency resolution: both identities are invariant under a commit whose
exact path set touches no writer surface and no verifier path. Re-verified in
both directions — the identities reproduce across the approval commit, and an
unrelated intervening writer-surface change rotates them and refuses.

The pass also confirmed the lifecycle itself: the bridge refuses an absent,
empty, unspecific, SHA-shaped and commit-valued authorization identically
whether `WFO-STATE-SERIALIZATION` derives `FAIL` or a hypothetical `PASS`; the
journal stays `schema_version` 3 carrying only the literal string; the bridge's
own approval commit moves `HEAD` with nothing asserting otherwise; the permanent
path runs without an authorization once the obligation is authorized; and it
falls back to the explicit window — rather than proceeding — the moment an
unreviewed serialization change appears.

### Pass 3 — "durability of the record, and does this break anything that already works?" (`R61-S3-001`, fixed)

A third perspective aimed at the *future* and at *regression*: what a later
workflow revision can do to an already-recorded verdict, whether the completion
gate can still be bypassed, and whether the new precondition makes any
legitimate existing path unreachable. 27 checks, including six run directly
against this repository's live state and declarations.

**`R61-S3-001`** — *authority as a blanket precondition would have broken
`D-Legacy`*. Checking the verifier authority of the work item *being completed*
rather than of the obligation's *owner* makes every `LEGACY_V1` import
permanently uncompletable: `D2` allows exactly that record shape to carry a null
`review_content_manifest`, and `D-Legacy`'s imported Milestone-8 entry declares
no obligation at all, so it would have been refused by a mechanism that does not
apply to it. Fixed: authority is resolved per declared obligation and from that
obligation's owner; a work item declaring none returns `(True, [])` without
consulting any approval; and `WFO-STATE-SERIALIZATION`'s authority is always
`workflow-v2-1-core`'s own approval, so approving another item's plan never
demands a technical approval of that item.

The pass additionally confirmed: replay executes the recorded verifier and is
unaffected by a later revision renaming the live derivation entry point out of
existence; an unreachable recorded verifier blob classifies
`REPLAY_UNRESOLVABLE` rather than falling back to live; registry-terminal plus
an unauthorized verifier does not complete; an empty verifier path set fails
closed; and — the regression question — `milestone_complete_gate_reachable` is
`True` only from `AWAITING_FUNCTIONAL_REVIEW`/`AWAITING_USER_ACCEPTANCE`, whose
only two writers are `apply_technical_approval` and `promote_legacy_work_item`,
so a technical approval already provably precedes the completion gate on every
reachable path and this binding introduces no unreachable state.

### Final state of the loop

Three repair cycles completed, which is the bound. All three passes were re-run
after the last repair and are green together: 25 + 32 + 27 = **84 checks, 0
failing**. No blocking or important defect remains outstanding in this
boundary. The one open condition — `docs/ai-workflow/dry-run/`'s missing
implementation-stage classification — is real, is validated, and is recorded as
item 359 rather than being applied unreviewed in a plan-only revision.

## Stress-pass findings (revision 60)

Three passes, three repairs, each pass re-run as a regression after every
repair. The bounded rule's cycle limit (three repair/stress cycles) is what ends
the loop. Every pass was **executed** — isolated scratch Git repositories, real
processes, real `flock` — not read for plausibility; 59 executable checks are
green across the three passes as of this revision.

The passes ran against a working prototype of this revision's mechanism rather
than against prose, and the same prototype was first used to reproduce all three
`GPT-R77` findings against revision 59's own stated rules. That ordering matters:
every fix below was demonstrated to close a defect that had been demonstrated to
exist.

### Pass 1 — "replay every revision-59 attack, then move the writer set" (`R60-S1-001`, `R60-S1-002`, both fixed)

Forged evidence in all three shapes, the add/remove/rename/change matrix, and
the unrelated-content non-staleness direction. Forgery is closed outright — a
hand-written `PASS` carrying the exact live digest, with an arbitrary or copied
`produced_by`, and a `FAILED` entry edited to `PASS`, all fail, and a legitimate
conformance passes whether such a file is absent, present, or says `FAILED`.
Two defects:

- **`R60-S1-001`** — the identity bound only the **declared-writer subset**. An
  *undeclared* file added to a writer surface correctly produced `FAIL` but left
  `obligation_content_id` unchanged, so two materially different repositories
  shared one identity. Nothing caches by identity today, so this was not
  exploitable — but the identity is exactly what the terminal transition records
  as its audit binding, and an audit binding that cannot distinguish two
  repositories is not one. Fixed by binding the **complete surface census**: an
  ordered `{path, blob}` entry for every tracked file on a declared surface,
  whatever it declares.
- **`R60-S1-002`** — the authoritative derivation and the worktree-sensitive
  resolution were the same function, so "a working-tree mutation cannot change
  the verdict" was not a statement the design could make. Fixed by factoring
  them apart: `derive_obligation_verdict(...)` reads only Git objects and is a
  pure function of `(obligation_id, commit)`; `resolve_obligation(...)` pins,
  applies the divergence precondition, and delegates. The precondition can now
  only ever *refuse*. Re-verified: with a verdict derived at pinned `C`,
  rewriting the helper, deleting a writer and planting an evidence-shaped file
  each left the verdict and its identity bit-for-bit unchanged, while a fresh
  resolve refused the same tree as `DIVERGED`.

### Pass 2 — "trust boundaries, discovery completeness, determinism" (`R60-S2-001`, `R60-S2-002`, both fixed)

A deliberately different angle: not *can the answer be forged*, but *can the
question be chosen*. Two defects:

- **`R60-S2-001`** — the gate took a **caller-supplied commit**, which is the
  `GPT-R37-001` shape this plan has already removed twice. With `HEAD` genuinely
  failing after a committed regression, handing the gate an ancestor commit at
  which the conformance passed returned `PASS` once the working tree was
  restored to that ancestor's content so the divergence precondition stayed
  silent. Fixed by removing the parameter: the gate resolves `HEAD` itself, and
  a caller that pinned earlier passes `expected_commit`, which **asserts**
  (`PIN_MOVED`) and never redirects.
- **`R60-S2-002`** — **namespaced commands were undiscovered.** Claude Code
  installs commands as `.claude/commands/<ns>/<name>.md`; a one-directory-level
  surface rule left an unlocked namespaced state writer entirely invisible and
  the gate returned `PASS` with it installed. Fixed by making surfaces
  recursive.

The same pass confirmed the properties this revision most needed to hold: a
symlinked file on a surface fails closed, a contradictory declaration fails
closed rather than being guessed at, the gate completes **with the live
`WORKFLOW_STATE.lock` actually held** and leaves it held, and the two consumers
returned identical verdicts on every state exercised.

### Pass 3 — "Git object resolution, conformance determinism, audit binding" (`R60-S3-001`, `R60-S3-002`, both fixed)

A third angle again: attack the substrate the design rests on rather than the
design. One defect and one hardening:

- **`R60-S3-001`** — **the behavioural conformance discriminated by luck.** A
  publisher that reads outside the critical section was rejected only because
  sixteen racing processes happened to interleave badly. A gate whose refusal
  depends on winning a race is not a gate, and a probabilistic conformance is a
  false-`PASS` generator with a small constant. Fixed by leading with a
  **deterministic barrier-based interleaving test**: a harness holds the lock,
  lets the writer start, publishes a value, then releases; a publisher reading
  inside the section necessarily preserves that value, one reading outside
  necessarily clobbers it. The N-way concurrency test is retained as an
  additional check, not as the discriminator. Verified 0/5 false passes,
  deterministically.
- **`R60-S3-002`** — **`git replace` refs rewrite what an object id resolves
  to**, which would break exactly the content-addressing this design rests on.
  Hardened: every Git read the gate performs uses `--no-replace-objects` with
  `GIT_NO_REPLACE_OBJECTS=1`. Exercised in both directions, including the
  dangerous one — substituting *honest* bytes over a failing blob is confirmed
  unable to launder that identity into a `PASS`.

Pass 3 also probed three discovery-surface escapes by installing a state-writing
file at each. Two were real: `scripts/rogue.bash` and
`.claude/commands/rogue.markdown` both escaped an extension-keyed surface rule
and both now refuse, the surfaces having been made extension-agnostic. The
third — hiding a writer as `scripts/*_test.py`, the one deliberate surface
exclusion — was examined and **deliberately not** classified as a defect: the
exclusion exists so unrelated test edits do not manufacture false staleness, and
the exploit path is closed elsewhere, because any command delegating its state
write to such a module fails the routing check. That is asserted directly rather
than argued (item 357(i)).

### Final state of the loop

Three repair cycles completed, which is the bound; **no blocking or important
defect remains unrepaired**, so the bound was reached with nothing outstanding
rather than with the standard weakened to finish. All three passes were re-run
in full after the last repair and are clean: the converted-repository model
resolves `PASS` over exactly twelve dynamically discovered writers; forged,
edited and deleted evidence records change no verdict; adding, removing,
renaming and rewriting writers each recompute the identity; unrelated content
does not; an ancestor commit cannot be smuggled in; the derivation is invariant
under working-tree mutation while a fresh resolve refuses it; the gate runs
inside the held state lock without deadlock; `git replace` cannot launder a
failing identity; and the terminal record replays exactly at its recorded
`source_commit`. Against this repository's *current* content the gate correctly
derives `FAIL` — item 354 has not landed — which is the honest pre-obligation
answer and a mechanical one, where revision 59 could only have reported an
absent record.

## Stress-pass findings (revision 59)

Five passes, three repairs, the last two clean. The bounded rule's cycle limit
(three repair/stress cycles) is what ends the loop.

### Pass 1 — "can the completion gate be bypassed, and does staleness bind to content?" (`R59-S1-001`, fixed)

The four evidence states, the quiescence/completion agreement, content-bound
staleness, the single terminal writer and a second synthetic obligation all
behaved as designed. The defect was in the helper signature this section itself
had just introduced: `resolve_completion_obligations(repo_root, work_item,
registry)` took a **caller-supplied registry**. That is precisely the trust
boundary `GPT-R37-001` removed from `complete_work_item` one layer up — a
caller could hand in a registry declaring no obligations at all and satisfy the
gate vacuously, exactly as it could once hand in one declaring every checkpoint
complete. Fixed the way this plan already fixed it once: **remove the trust
boundary rather than tighten a check on it.** Both the registry and the evidence
artifact are now resolved internally from `repo_root` and the work item's own
declared paths, through the same authoritative resolution
`resolve_own_registry_completion_status` performs — including its plan-approval
coverage check, which as a side effect means an obligation cannot be added or
made to disappear by an unapproved registry edit.

### Pass 2 — "is index-only staging really harmless after journal close?" (clean)

Each of the four remaining `"ordinary"` guards was exercised against real Git
with its operation delayed until after the replacement owner's transaction
completed, after journal close, and after a legal foreign state write. For all
four: `HEAD` unmoved, approval commit intact, state file unchanged, the foreign
update intact, the residue exactly one staged path, and `git diff --cached
--quiet` non-clean so the next run's index-isolation precondition refuses. The
"harmless in every state reachable after journal close" clause holds as written.

### Pass 3 — "does this revision obey its own rule?" (`R59-S3-001`, fixed)

Applying `GPT-R76-001`'s and `GPT-R76-002`'s rule to the new completion gate
itself: every transition helper is a pure `state -> new_state` function whose
result the *calling command* persists, so the gate ran in the helper while the
publication happened in the caller — putting the gate's reads outside the
critical section and the write inside it, which is the shape `GPT-R76-002`
forbids for ordinary writers and the "an earlier verification exists" fallacy
`GPT-R76-001` forbids for guarded mutations. Fixed by requiring the obligation
evaluation, the registry completion resolution and the state publication to be
**one critical section**. The same pass added the lock-ordering rule: where both
the mutation guard and the state-file `flock` are held — step 8b, the only such
place — the order is guard-then-`flock` on every path, so inversion is
unreachable by construction.

### Pass 4 — "does the pass-3 fix compose?" (clean)

Verified mechanically that no function the gate calls reads the state file from
disk (the state dict is passed in) or shells out, so evaluating the gate inside
the critical section triggers no second acquisition and never meets `D1`'s
explicit re-entrancy refusal. The terminal-phase writer set is still exactly
`complete_work_item`.

### Pass 5 — "system-level: does anything added here break what it must preserve?" (`R59-S5-001`, fixed)

Validators, identity resolution, the other two work items, and `"1"`-governance
compatibility all held; the obligation is declared in exactly one registry
repository-wide. The defect was in item 355's own clause (b), which this
revision had inherited and rewritten: "no missing-test item whose owner resolves
to a `COMPLETE` checkpoint is left without an overriding umbrella entry, checked
across the whole list" is **unsatisfiable** — run against the live plan and
state it flags 83 items, every one numbered below 167, all of them historical
obligations that the checkpoint named in their suffix actually implemented
before completing. A conformance that can never pass is worse than none: it
either blocks `WF8b` forever or gets quietly weakened during implementation.
Rescoped to the continued-scope era — every item ≥ 167 must fall within the
umbrella, and no item may be *added* with an owner suffix resolving to a
`COMPLETE` checkpoint unless the umbrella covers it — which returns empty
against the live plan while still catching exactly the failure revision 57
demonstrated.

### Final state of the loop

Three repair cycles completed, which is the bound. The two passes after the last
repair were re-run in full and are clean: item 355(b) returns empty, the
umbrella's upper bound equals the highest item, numbering has no gaps, items
354-356 are owned by `WF8b`, `select_next_checkpoint` reaches `WF8b`,
`registry_completion_status` is `(False, "WF8b")`, `WF8b` declares the
obligation, plan/registry/state agree on revision 59, `governing_workflow_version`

## WF8b finding disposition (revision 57 → 58) — external plan review confirmed `GPT-R74-001` and `-003` resolved but found ownership *transfer* still unfenced, the temporary bridge still claiming a safety it does not have, and the obligation behind that safety owned by an already-complete checkpoint (`GPT-R75-001`/`-002`/`-003`)

External plan review of revision 57 returned `Status: REVISE`, **zero blocking
findings and three important findings**. The reviewer independently reproduced
`bundle_id` `80746937…` from a fresh archive extraction, rebuilt the plan-stage
projection from first principles to `review_content_id` `e34e74fa…`, confirmed
the 63-row plan/mapping normalization zero-mismatch, and reran all 489 hermetic
tests green. `GPT-R74-001` was closed for its principal publication and
explicit-ownership design, `GPT-R74-003` closed outright, and every earlier
round's resolution left standing.

All three findings were **validated against this repository before acceptance,
never taken on the finding's own premise**, and all three were accepted. No
finding was rejected.

### `GPT-R75-001` — important — `assert_owner` is a check-before-mutation, not an ownership barrier

Accepted in full, and reproduced twice: once to confirm the defect, once to
confirm the fix.

The plan text was read first. Revision 57 said `assert_owner` "runs immediately
before every step that mutates Git, the index, `WORKFLOW_STATE.json`, or the
journal," and the takeover contract's step (4) re-verified `owner_token` and
`step_seq` and step (5) rotated. Nothing made those two sequences exclusive of
each other — confirmed by reading, not inferred. A scratch harness then
reproduced the exact interleaving the finding names, with real threads and the
real primitives (`os.link` no-replace publication, `os.replace` rotation):

```
owner_assert(T) OK → takeover_reverify(T) OK → takeover_rotate(T2) → owner_mutate
```

Final state: journal `owner_token == T2`, target written by the **displaced**
owner. The finding's claim that `step_seq` cannot close this was confirmed
directly — the owner advanced nothing between its assertion and its mutation,
so the takeover's staleness evidence was legitimately unchanged.

The fix is the **transaction mutation/handoff guard**
(`.ai-review/runtime/PLAN_APPROVAL_MUTATION.lease`), a single fixed pathname
acquired by the same atomic, complete, no-replace `os.link` publication the
journal uses. Its whole content is an ordering change plus an exclusion:
`assert_owner` moves **inside** the guard, the guard is held through the
mutation and the progress-record update, and **takeover acquires the same
guard** before its re-verification and holds it through the rotation. A second
token read before the mutation was explicitly rejected as the fix, exactly as
the finding required: it only shrinks the same window.

Running the identical interleaving against the guarded contract produced:

```
owner_acquire_guard → owner_assert(T) OK (under guard)
  → takeover_refused (guard held) → owner_mutate (under guard) → owner_release_guard
```

with the journal still carrying `T`, the target written by its rightful owner,
and the takeover acquiring normally once the owner released. Three further
properties were reproduced: a displaced owner resuming after a *completed*
takeover acquires a guard, fails `assert_owner` inside it, releases and stops
without mutating; twelve concurrent guard contenders produce exactly one
winner; and a guard left behind by a superseded epoch is reclaimed
deterministically with no authorization and no wall-clock read.

Three design points are worth stating because they are where this could have
gone wrong:

- **Takeover refuses rather than waits**, with an explicitly bounded rule —
  exactly one acquisition attempt, no retry, no timeout, no wall clock. A held
  guard is *positive* evidence the owner is live at that instant, which is
  strictly better evidence than the `step_seq` comparison the takeover already
  performs.
- **A `"destructive"` step class is never breakable, by any authorization.** It
  covers exactly the rollback's whole-index `git reset --mixed HEAD` and journal
  deletion — the only two mutations for which no downstream check could catch a
  displaced owner completing them. This is what makes the finding's required
  correction (7) mechanically true rather than merely asserted.
- **The residual is stated rather than papered over.** Breaking an `"ordinary"`
  same-epoch guard cannot revoke a running session's next syscall; no POSIX
  primitive can, and claiming otherwise would be the same class of absolute
  statement this finding was raised against. So the plan bounds the blast radius
  to a single step and enumerates, one by one, why every member of that bounded
  set is detected (index staging by sub-steps 6.3/6.4; `git commit` by the
  outcome classifier; the amend by step 7's three checks) or harmless (step 8b's
  byte-identical idempotent write; the token-scoped progress record) — and why
  the two destructive ones are unreachable.

### `GPT-R75-002` — important — "never merges" is not a compare-and-swap

Accepted in full. Reproduced exactly as the finding describes, and then
reproduced again in the configuration the finding did not need but this
revision did: **with the bridge holding
`.ai-review/runtime/WORKFLOW_STATE.lock`**. The result was identical, which is
the whole point — an advisory lock is worth nothing against a writer that does
not take it:

```
final re-read observes milestone-8.state_revision == 7
  → unlocked foreign writer publishes state_revision == 8
  → bridge whole-file os.replace(expected_post_state_b64)
  → published file carries state_revision == 7
```

Revision 57's disposition sentence — "A step that never reads-and-rewrites
foreign content cannot lose foreign content, whether or not the other writer
cooperates" — is therefore **withdrawn**, in `D1`, in step 8b, and in the
revision-57 status block and disposition section, each corrected in place with
the superseded claim left visible rather than quietly rewritten, since it was
this bridge's load-bearing safety argument. What survives is the true, narrower
statement: not merging removes the class in which *this step itself* republishes
stale foreign bytes. Step 8b's final re-read is likewise renamed from
"compare-and-swap on a fresh read" to what it is — a detection check.

The replacement is not a mechanism, because no honest mechanism is available
here, and the finding said so: this plan does not assemble "check hash, then
`os.replace`" and call it a CAS. Instead the two contracts are separated
explicitly, as the finding required.

**Temporary bridge** — a user-authorized **state-writer quiescence window**:

- **authorized** by a current-turn literal confirmation naming
  `workflow-v2-1-core` and the `plan` stage, required at **step 4a** and
  recorded verbatim in the journal's new `quiescence_authorization` field
  (`schema_version` `2 → 3`), so the authority is durable and a fresh-session
  forward completion inherits it and cannot materialize state without it;
- **refuses outright** when absent — placed at step 4a rather than step 8b
  precisely so that *no* mutation of any kind ever occurs under an unauthorized
  window;
- **starts** at journal publication and **ends** at journal close, staying open
  across every branch that deliberately leaves the journal in place — the
  journal's existence *is* the window's durable marker, so there is no branch on
  which it ends silently;
- **prohibits** all twelve installed state-writing commands, in any session and
  any worktree sharing this repository, plus any manual edit;
- **binds reconciliation to the same rule**, since both reconciliations step 8b
  can require are themselves writes of the shared file — otherwise the identical
  race simply relocates, which is the finding's required correction (2);
- **states its violation behavior without euphemism**: the window is an
  authorization, not a lock; a write landing between the final re-read and the
  `os.replace` is a violation, is **outside** the bridge's safe execution
  contract, can lose that writer's update, and is reported as a state-loss
  incident with a stated Git-based recovery — never as a loss-free race. No
  in-contract execution contains that interleaving, because no in-contract
  execution contains a concurrent writer at all.

**Permanent mechanism** — item 354, now reachable (see `GPT-R75-003`), makes
every supported writer acquire the primitive. `D1` gains an explicit
three-state transition (unlocked-and-quiescent → item 354 lands as a single
all-or-nothing conversion → lock becomes the mechanism and quiescence retires),
with a stated absence of any fourth state in which concurrent writes are called
safe while some supported writer still ignores the primitive. Item 347 gains a
**second pairing rule** forbidding the permanent command from dropping the
quiescence precondition except in the same change that lands item 354.

**A load-bearing factual error was found while enumerating the prohibited
writers, and corrected.** Revision 57 stated three times that **eight**
installed commands write `docs/ai-workflow/WORKFLOW_STATE.json`. Verified
directly against `.claude/commands/`, the number is **twelve**;
`/prepare-review` is the sole non-writer, and no file under `scripts/` writes
the path at all (`workflow_state.py` has no state-file writer, which is why
every writer is a command file). The four omitted are `/apply-plan-review`'s
own `"2.1"` exit branch, `/review-plan`, `/record-manual-plan-review` and
`/accept-scoped-remediation` — and the middle two are live **today** for the
`"2.1"` `v2-1-dry-run` work item that currently holds `active_work_item_id`, so
an eight-name list would have under-specified both the quiescence window and
item 354's completeness assertion. Item 354 is correspondingly strengthened to
assert the enumeration **against the live `.claude/commands/` directory** rather
than against the plan's own list, so a writer added later cannot pass by being
absent from prose.

### `GPT-R75-003` — important — item 354 had no reachable implementation owner

Accepted in full, and validated against every source the finding names rather
than against its text. `docs/ai-workflow/WORKFLOW_STATE.json` records
`WF4a-iii.status == COMPLETE`; the protected registry lists all 17 checkpoints;
`workflow_state.select_next_checkpoint(...)` was executed against that live
state and registry and returned **`WF8b`**, not `WF4a-iii`; and the "Missing
tests" umbrella was confirmed to read `items 167-353`, one short of revision
57's own new item 354. The finding's reading was correct in every particular.

The smallest correction consistent with this plan's own `GPT-R29-003`
precedent — item 166, found assigned to already-complete `WF8a-ii`, reassigned
to `WF8b` continued scope rather than reopening the checkpoint — is the one
applied:

1. item 354's owner changes `→ WF4a-iii` to `→ WF8b`, with the reasoning and the
   executed selector result recorded in the item itself;
2. the continued-scope umbrella extends `167-353` → `167-355`;
3. `WF8b` is stated unable to complete while item 354 is unsatisfied, which is
   what makes the quiescence window's retirement condition unskippable;
4. `WFR-63`'s verification column gains an explicit ownership note: that row's
   `WF4a-iii` owns the revision-50 conditional-fifth-member property it was
   written for and nothing more, and the forward-looking obligations it
   *mentions* are owned by their own checkpoints — item 354 by `WF8b`, never by
   this already-complete one;
5. `WF4a-iii` is **not** reopened.

New item 355 turns reachability itself into a conformance obligation: the
selector is run for real and must reach a checkpoint owning item 354; no item
may be owned only by a `COMPLETE` checkpoint without an overriding umbrella
entry, checked across the whole list rather than for the newest item; the
umbrella's upper bound must equal the list's highest item, so adding an item
without extending the range fails rather than silently orphaning it; `WF8b`'s
inability to complete with item 354 outstanding is exercised through
`registry_completion_status(...)`/`resolve_own_registry_completion_status(...)`
rather than asserted in prose; and requirements-row wording is checked for the
inheritance implication this finding caught.

Items 348-353 already carried historical `→ WF4a-iii` suffixes overridden by the
umbrella; revision 58 additionally updates those suffixes in place to `→ WF8b`
so the suffix and the umbrella agree rather than requiring a reader to know the
umbrella overrides them.

### Stress passes

Three bounded adversarial stress passes were run over the resulting
approval/bootstrap transaction, from deliberately different failure-mode
perspectives. Passes 1 and 2 each found one concrete defect in this same
contract, both validated and fixed here; pass 3 found none. See "Stress-pass
findings (revision 58)" below.

### Scope

Nothing outside this transaction contract was changed. The reviewer's
"Confirmed resolutions" for `GPT-R74-001`/`-003`, `GPT-R73-*`, `GPT-R72-001`,
`GPT-R71-001`, `GPT-R70-001`, `GPT-R69-001`, `GPT-R68-001`, `GPT-R67-001`,
`GPT-R65-001`, `GPT-R64-*`, `GPT-R63-002` and the R62 corrections are left
untouched. Revision 57's link publication, durable `owner_token`,
refuse-by-default/explicit-takeover model, index-pinned state, exact
expected-post-state binding, committed-state-byte verification, exact committed
path set, declaration binding and exhaustive three-check post-amend verification
all survive intact except where strengthened above; no automatic recovery by
arbitrary sessions is reintroduced, and no long-lived process `flock` assumption
appears anywhere — `fcntl.flock` remains used nowhere in this contract, and item
347's own stale revision-56 `flock` wording is corrected to match (stress pass
1). `WORKFLOW_STATE.json`'s round-9 fields
(`reviewed_implementation_head`/`implementation_revision`/`technical_approval`)
are left exactly as recorded, through revisions 28 through 58. No new `WFR` row
and no `WFR` description change: `WFR-63`'s acceptance/test column carries this
round, so `workflow-v2-1-core-mapping.json`'s descriptions are unaffected and
the 63-row plan/mapping normalization stays zero-mismatch.

## Stress-pass findings (revision 58)

Three passes, each from a different perspective, per the bounded rule: stop
after two consecutive clean passes or three repair cycles.

### Pass 1 — "does every obligation still say what the contract now says?"

**`R58-S1-001` (important, fixed)** — missing-test item 347's own text still
required the permanent `/approve-review` to carry "exclusive `flock`-based
journal acquisition," revision 56's form, even though revision 57 replaced it
with atomic no-replace `os.link` publication and stated that `fcntl.flock` is
used nowhere in this contract. `D-Approval-Commits` step 11 had recorded the
supersession; item 347 had not. An implementer working from the missing-test
list — which is the artifact `WF8b`'s acceptance is actually measured against —
would have been told to build the retired primitive, and the conformance
assertion would have passed on it. Fixed in place, with the supersession
recorded rather than the history erased. This is the same failure mode
`GPT-R74-003` found in step 7's own "both checks" wording, at a different site.

### Pass 2 — "can the new guard itself be turned against the transaction?"

Seven probes were run against a faithful implementation of the guard's stated
rules, with real threads and one real subprocess. Six confirmed the rules hold:
a takeover cannot claim an owner's in-flight guard as its own leftover (the
reuse rule is scoped to the session that *holds* the current token, and a
takeover holds none until it rotates); a `"destructive"` guard is refused even
against a byte-matching guard-release authorization; a stale authorization
quoting a superseded `lease_id` is refused as proof the owner is live; a
matching authorization does release an `"ordinary"` guard, so required
correction (6) is reachable; a superseded-epoch guard is reclaimed by the new
owner with no authorization; a guard outlives its holder process and is
recovered by the owner's own reuse rule; and sixteen concurrent contenders
produced exactly one winner with no partially-written guard ever observed.

**`R58-S2-001` (important, fixed)** — the seventh probe found a real defect
this revision introduced. Several guarded steps flow directly into the
approval-transaction rollback, whose own operations are separately guarded:
sub-step 6.1c's digest mismatch, sub-step 6's `NOT_COMMITTED` classification,
and step 5's pin mismatch. As first drafted, those steps held their
`"ordinary"` guard across the verification that decides to roll back — so the
rollback's `"destructive"` acquisition ran while the same session still held a
guard. Independently reproduced: the nested `os.link` fails, because the guard
is a pathname and not a recursive lock; and the same-epoch owner-reuse rule
degrades that into an `os.unlink`-then-`os.link` pair whose gap a concurrent
takeover **was observed to win**, after which the rollback could acquire
nothing and the transaction stalled with a staged index and no recovery path.
The new guard would have created a stall the old contract did not have.

Fixed by an explicit rule rather than by adjusting the four call sites
individually: **guard windows are strictly non-nested and non-reentrant, and
cover the mutation plus its progress-record update only** — never a following
verification, classification or comparison, all of which are pure reads. Every
entry into the rollback is therefore from a guard-free state. Sub-steps 6.1b,
6.5, 7(b) and 7(d) were each restated accordingly. Releasing before the
classification is safe for a reason the plan already relies on elsewhere: the
classifier reads durable Git state only, a takeover acquiring the guard in that
gap runs the same classifier from its own step 0 and reaches the same answer,
and the displaced session's next act is a guarded step whose `assert_owner`
fails inside the guard, so it releases and stops. Exactly one session ever
performs the rollback.

Separately and non-defect: the release ordering at step 8a and at rollback (5)
was made explicit — the guard is released **after** the journal, the progress
record and the claim links — closing the window in which the journal is gone
while a takeover could still believe it may act.

### Pass 3 — "crash/recovery boundaries and provenance, against real Git"

No blocking or important defect found. Four probes were run against real
scratch repositories and against this repository's own live state and registry,
rather than reasoned from the plan text:

1. **Index-pinned staging.** `git hash-object -w --path` plus `git update-index
   --add --cacheinfo` left the working-tree `docs/ai-workflow/WORKFLOW_STATE.json`
   byte-unchanged, the mode was read from `HEAD` as `100644` rather than
   assumed, and a plain pathspec-free `git commit` committed exactly the pinned
   bytes. Revision 56's architecture is intact under revision 58's guard
   ordering.
2. **Same-path hook mutation across an amend.** A `pre-commit` hook that
   rewrote and re-staged only `WORKFLOW_STATE.json` produced an amended commit
   whose path set was identical to the pre-amend commit's and whose state bytes
   were the hook's; the amend preserved the first parent, so the classifier's
   `first parent == pre_procedure_head` test still holds. Confirms that step
   7's committed-state-bytes check is the only one of the three that catches
   this, exactly as `GPT-R74-003` established and revision 58 preserves.
3. **Index isolation.** Unrelated pre-staged content is visible to the exact
   staged-path-set check before any journal is opened or anything is staged, so
   it fails closed rather than riding into an approval commit.
4. **Checkpoint reachability for every newly-owned obligation.**
   `select_next_checkpoint(...)` run against the live state and registry returns
   `WF8b`; `WF4a-iii` is `COMPLETE`; `WF8b` is present in the registry and is
   not complete; and `registry_completion_status(...)` reports the work item
   incomplete with `WF8b` outstanding — so items 354 and 355 are reachable and
   `WF8b` cannot complete around them.

Interruption at each new guard boundary resolves through an already-enumerated
rule: before acquisition, nothing happened; inside the window, the guard is
same-epoch (the sole owner reuses it) or superseded-epoch (deterministically
reclaimed, no authorization, no wall clock); after the mutation but before
release, the progress record and the guard together describe the state and the
next session's `assert_owner` decides. Takeover crashes resolve through the
existing claim-link rule plus the superseded-epoch guard rule, since a
takeover's guard carries the token it is superseding. All load-bearing bindings
— separately-bound excluded content, exact reviewed declaration bytes, exact
expected post-approval state bytes, exact committed path membership, same-path
hook detectability, exclusion of unrelated staged content, exhaustive
post-amend verification, and fresh-session recovery refusing an unresolved or
invalid transaction — were re-checked against the edited text and are unchanged
in effect. The temporary bridge remains compatible with `workflow-v2-1-core`
permanently carrying `governing_workflow_version: "1"`: nothing added this
revision touches `WORKFLOW_STATE.json`'s schema, so the file stays readable by
the unmodified v1 commands throughout.

Per the bounded rule, the cycle stops here: two repair cycles, three passes, the
final pass clean. No blocking or important issue remains unrepaired.

## Decisions (revision 22)

### D-Bootstrap — one-time Workflow-v1-to-v2.1 transition (new, resolves GPT-R9-004)

Every other section in this document describes behavior `/approve-review`,
multi-item `WORKFLOW_STATE.json`, and the rest of v2.1's own machinery will
have once built. None of it exists yet in this repository: today's
`/milestone-plan`/`/milestone-implement`/`/apply-plan-review` are the
unmodified v1 commands, `docs/ACTIVE_MILESTONE.md`/`docs/ROADMAP.md` still
point at Milestone 8, and this milestone's own working tree already
contains fully-reviewed, not-yet-committed content (the prototype scripts,
CI wiring, the technical-decision entry, the registry/mapping JSON files,
and this plan/audit pair themselves) with no commit lifecycle defined for
any of it — round 9 correctly found this the actual precondition gap
before implementation can start at all, not a detail deferrable into WF1a.

**Why this cannot be solved by extending an existing command.**
`/milestone-implement` (v1, today) selects work by reading
`docs/ACTIVE_MILESTONE.md`/`docs/ROADMAP.md`, which this milestone is an
explicit non-goal to touch. Modifying `/milestone-implement` itself to
recognize the process plan would require exactly the work-item routing
(D1) that doesn't exist until WF1b lands — circular. The bootstrap path is
therefore necessarily a separate, temporary, narrowly-scoped mechanism,
retired once real infrastructure exists.

**WF0 — the bootstrap checkpoint** (first in the registry, depends on
nothing, complexity 2/Small):
