      **next** run of this procedure refuses on at step 3's index-isolation
      precondition rather than absorbing. Nothing is lost and nothing is
      silently accepted.
    That is a real "harmless in every state reachable after journal close,"
    not an appeal to a check that may already have run.

  - **A `"destructive"` guard abandoned in the current epoch has no in-band
    resolution, and that is deliberate** (revision 59). A takeover finding
    one refuses and reports that no authorization can release it. The stated
    resolutions are resuming in the owning session or an **out-of-band
    manual guard clearance**: the user establishes, outside this procedure,
    that the holding session is genuinely gone — closing the session, or
    confirming the process no longer exists — and only then removes
    `.ai-review/runtime/PLAN_APPROVAL_MUTATION.lease` by hand. This is
    categorically different from the in-band break below: the user is
    asserting a fact about process liveness they can actually verify, rather
    than the procedure inferring liveness from a file it cannot interpret.
    Nothing about the transaction is lost by the wait — the journal, its
    bound pre/post state, and the durable Git record are all intact, and the
    next session's step 0 classifies and completes forward or rolls back
    exactly as it would have.

  - **An `"ordinary"` guard abandoned in the current epoch** is the one case
    with an in-band resolution (`GPT-R75-001`'s required correction (6)). It
    is released only through the takeover contract's **guard-release
    authorization** — a distinct literal confirmation quoting the exact
    observed `lease_id`, `holder_owner_token`, `step` and `step_class`,
    supplied in the same turn as the takeover authorization — and only when
    the guard is re-observed byte-identical to the quoted one at claim time
    (a changed `lease_id` proves the owner released and re-acquired, i.e. is
    live: refuse). This is the same "quote it, then re-observe it unchanged"
    standard the journal takeover already applies to `step_seq`/`updated_at`,
    applied to the guard.

  - **The residual, stated exactly rather than papered over.** Breaking an
    `"ordinary"` same-epoch guard cannot make a displaced-but-alive owner's
    already-issued next operation fail: no POSIX primitive revokes a running
    session's ability to call `write` or `execve`, and claiming otherwise
    would be exactly the kind of absolute assertion `GPT-R75-001` was raised
    against. What this design does instead is confine the breakable set to
    operations that write **only the Git index** and then discharge the
    "harmless after close" clause for that set explicitly, above. The
    remaining residual is therefore: after a user's own literal
    guard-release authorization, one already-issued **index staging**
    operation may still land, and its worst reachable outcome is a dirty
    index that the next run refuses on. No mutation of Git history and no
    write of the shared state file is reachable through a break at all,
    because none of them is breakable any more.

  **Refuse by default; takeover is explicit (new, revision 57,
  `GPT-R74-001`, required corrections (4) and (5))**. A session that
  encounters a **valid, complete** journal whose `owner_token` it does not
  hold must **not** roll it back, complete it forward, replace it, or delete
  it. It refuses, reports, and offers exactly two resolutions: resume in the
  owning session, or take over explicitly. Takeover is the only ownership
  transfer, and it is mechanically defined:
  1. **Observe.** Read the journal, the owner progress record, **and the
     mutation guard** (revision 58). Report to the user: the journal's
     `owner_token` `T`, the progress record's `step_seq`/`updated_at` (or
     its absence), the guard's `lease_id`/`step`/`step_class` (or its
     absence), the read-only outcome classification, and what a takeover
     would do next.
  2. **Authorize.** Require the user's own current-turn literal takeover
     confirmation naming `workflow-v2-1-core`, the `plan` stage, the exact
     observed `owner_token` `T`, and the exact observed `step_seq` (or the
     literal `none`). This is the same class of user-only gate step 1
     already imposes, and it is what makes takeover an *authorization*
     rather than an inference. **When a guard was observed** (revision 58,
     `GPT-R75-001`), the confirmation must additionally carry the separate
     **guard-release authorization**, quoting the exact observed `lease_id`,
     `holder_owner_token`, `step` and `step_class`. A confirmation that
     quotes a `step_class` of `"destructive"` is **refused outright** — that
     guard is never breakable, by anyone (see the guard contract above), and
     no wording of an authorization changes that. As of revision 59 that
     covers every mutation of Git history and of the shared state file, so
     the only guards this authorization can ever release are index-only
     staging ones.
  3. **Claim, exclusively.** `os.link(<journal path>,
     <runtime>/PLAN_APPROVAL_JOURNAL.claim.<T>)`. The claim name embeds the
     exact observed token, so the claim is scoped to this one ownership
     epoch; `FileExistsError` means another session is already taking this
     same transaction over — refuse, having mutated nothing. Independently
     reproduced: eight concurrent takeover attempts against one journal
     produced exactly one winner.
  3a. **Acquire the mutation guard (new, revision 58, `GPT-R75-001`)** —
     the same fixed-path, no-replace `os.link` guard every mutating step
     acquires, with `holder_owner_token: T`, `step: "takeover"`,
     `step_class: "ordinary"`. Exactly one attempt:
     - **Acquired**: hold it through (4) and (5), and release it at (5a).
       This is what makes the re-verification and the rotation mutually
       exclusive with any owner's `assert_owner + mutation` window.
     - **`FileExistsError`, superseded epoch** (the held guard's
       `holder_owner_token` is not the journal's current `owner_token`):
       remove it and retry acquisition once, per the guard contract.
     - **`FileExistsError`, current epoch, `step_class: "destructive"`**:
       refuse, unconditionally and unbreakably; report which destructive step
       the owner is inside — as of revision 59 that is the commit, the amend,
       the state-file materialization, the rollback's index reset, or a
       journal close — and that the only resolutions are resuming in the
       owning session or the out-of-band manual guard clearance the guard
       contract defines (establish, outside this procedure, that the holding
       session is genuinely gone, then remove the guard by hand). No
       authorization supplied to this procedure releases such a guard.
     - **`FileExistsError`, current epoch, `step_class: "ordinary"`, guard
       byte-identical to the one step (2)'s guard-release authorization
       quoted**: the authorized break. Remove the guard and retry
       acquisition once.
     - **`FileExistsError`, current epoch, `step_class: "ordinary"`, guard
       *not* byte-identical to the quoted one** (a different `lease_id`):
       the owner released and re-acquired between authorization and claim
       and is therefore demonstrably **live** — refuse, mutate nothing,
       report that the transaction is progressing.
     No branch here waits, loops, or consults a wall clock.
  4. **Re-verify before rotating, under the guard.** Re-read the journal and
     require `owner_token == T` still, and re-read the progress record and
     require `step_seq`/`updated_at` to be exactly the values the
     authorization quoted. Either having advanced proves the owner is
     **live**: mutate nothing, release the guard, refuse, and report that the
     transaction is progressing. (Under revision 58 this check is a
     defence-in-depth backstop rather than the primary exclusion mechanism —
     the guard is — but it is retained because it is the only check that
     catches an owner that made progress and released the guard entirely
     between step (1)'s observation and step (3a)'s acquisition.)
  5. **Rotate, still under the guard.** Serialize a new journal body — every
     transaction field carried over byte-identically, `owner_token` set to a
     fresh 32-hex token `T'`, `takeover_count` incremented, `T` appended to
     `previous_owner_tokens` — to a temporary file in the same directory,
     `fsync` it, and `os.replace` it onto the journal path. `os.replace` is
     correct here, and only here, because step (3)'s claim already
     serialized every contender for epoch `T` and step (3a)'s guard excludes
     every concurrent mutation. `fsync` the directory. The claim link remains
     as the durable, self-describing takeover record: it is a hard link to
     the pre-takeover inode, so the superseded journal's exact bytes stay
     readable for audit.
  5a. **Release the guard (new, revision 58).** `os.unlink` the guard;
     `FileNotFoundError` is success. Note that the guard's own
     `holder_owner_token` is `T`, which the rotation at (5) has just made a
     superseded token — so even a session that dies between (5) and (5a)
     leaves a guard the new owner reclaims deterministically under the
     superseded-epoch rule, with no authorization and no wall clock.
  6. **Proceed as owner.** The taking-over session now holds `T'` and runs
     the *same* outcome classifier and the *same* forward-completion or
     rollback logic an uninterrupted owner would — required correction (5).
     Nothing about the classifier, the rollback, or steps 7-9 changes; only
     who is authorized to run them. Every mutating step it runs acquires the
     mutation guard exactly as an uninterrupted owner's would.
  A crash inside the takeover is bounded and deterministic, because steps
  (1)-(4) mutate nothing durable and step (5) is a single atomic replace:
  either the journal still carries `T` (the takeover never happened) or it
  carries `T'` (it did). If a claim link exists for `T` while the journal
  still carries `T`, the claiming session died before rotating; since a
  mid-claim session provably mutated nothing, a fresh takeover — with its own
  fresh authorization — may `os.unlink` that claim (`FileNotFoundError` is
  success) and retry from (3), where `os.link` again admits exactly one
  winner. This terminates: there is no ladder of ever-longer names. A guard
  left behind by that same dead claimer carries `holder_owner_token: T` and
  `step: "takeover"`, so it is either reclaimed by the superseded-epoch rule
  (if some rotation did land) or covered by the fresh takeover's own
  guard-release authorization (if none did) — and never by a destructive-step
  refusal, since a takeover's own guard is always `"ordinary"`.

  What this changes about the residual concurrency argument (revision 56
  claimed the interleaving "fails closed"; revision 57 makes it *impossible*
  rather than merely survivable):
  - a second **run** of this procedure still refuses at step 4a, because
    publication is exclusive;
  - a second **recovery** session now refuses at step 0 as well, because it
    does not hold the journal's `owner_token` and no automatic path grants
    it one;
  - a live owner therefore cannot have its journal deleted, rolled back,
    completed, or replaced by any **unauthorized** session, in any window,
    including the publication window that no longer exists. The one
    remaining way a live transaction changes hands is a takeover the user
    explicitly authorizes after being shown that owner's own progress
    evidence — and even then, the takeover refuses if that evidence
    advanced in the meantime, and the displaced owner fails its very next
    `assert_owner` and stops rather than continuing to mutate. That
    residual is a human decision with a mechanical staleness check in
    front of it and a fail-closed backstop behind it, not an inference the
    procedure makes on its own; it is stated here rather than papered over
    with an absolute claim;
  - **(revision 58, `GPT-R75-001`)** "the displaced owner fails its very
    next `assert_owner`" is true only of an assertion made *after* the
    rotation, and revision 57 relied on it to cover an assertion made
    *before* one. That gap is now closed by the mutation guard rather than
    by the sentence: ownership can only rotate while the guard is held, the
    guard is held across every `assert_owner + mutation` window, and the two
    therefore cannot interleave. What remains is the explicitly authorized,
    explicitly bounded, individually-checked guard-break residual the guard
    contract enumerates above — and never for a destructive step;
  - and a genuinely abandoned transaction is still recoverable — through an
    explicit, user-authorized takeover whose staleness evidence is checked
    mechanically rather than assumed, and whose guard-release, when one is
    needed at all, is authorized separately and refused outright for a
    destructive step.

  This is deliberately *not* the mechanism relied on to stop the installed
  `/bootstrap-workflow-v2` command, which reads no journal at all. That
  command is handled structurally instead — see "No usable partial approval
  state" below.

  Its fields are
  `schema_version` (`3`, bumped from `2` by revision 58's
  `quiescence_authorization` field, itself bumped from `1` by revision 57's
  three ownership fields — the journal is local-only and never migrated, so
  a journal declaring any other version is refused outright rather than
  upgraded); `owner_token`, `takeover_count`, `previous_owner_tokens` (all
  new, revision 57, `GPT-R74-001` — see "Transaction ownership" above);
  `quiescence_authorization` (new, revision 58, `GPT-R75-002` — the user's
  literal state-writer quiescence authorization text, recorded here so that
  the window's authority is durable and a fresh-session forward completion
  inherits it rather than silently materializing state without one; see
  "Temporary state-writer quiescence window" below. **It is a non-empty
  string carrying that literal text and nothing else — never a commit, never
  a commit carried alongside the text, and never any other encoded value**
  (revision 61, `GPT-R78-002`: `schema_version` stays `3` precisely because
  the field's type and meaning are unchanged; revision 60's prose claiming
  this field also carried the bridge's pinned commit is withdrawn, and no
  schema bump or second typed field is needed once the bridge stops pinning
  at all));
  `work_item_id`; `stage` (`"plan"`);
  `repo_root`/`git_common_dir`/`worktree_root` (the same worktree-identity
  triple `WORKTREE_IDENTITY.json` records, read from the same live-Git
  source); `pre_procedure_head` (the 40-hex `git rev-parse HEAD` taken
  before any mutation); `pre_procedure_state_b64` (the exact pre-procedure
  `WORKFLOW_STATE.json` bytes, base64-encoded so the exact byte sequence
  survives JSON round-tripping unchanged) together with
  `pre_procedure_state_sha256` (their sha256, so restoration is verifiable
  independently of the encoding); `base_commit` (the work item's own
  declared `base_commit`, copied here because the outcome classifier needs
  it to scope its trailer lookup and must not have to re-read it from
  `WORKFLOW_STATE.json`, the one file whose trustworthiness the classifier
  exists to be independent of — `apply_plan_approval` does not touch
  `base_commit`, so re-reading it would in fact be harmless, but depending
  on that fact would make the classifier's independence an accident rather
  than a property); `expected_bundle_id` and `expected_review_content_id`
  (step 2's freshly recomputed values — the first binds the transaction to
  the exact reviewed round for reporting and audit, the second is the
  classifier's own trailer-lookup key); `applicable_paths` (the sorted,
  repo-relative file set step 4 determined); `fifth_member_applies`;
  `fifth_member_sha256` (the sha256 of the reviewed declaration bytes, read
  **once** here from the bundle's own captured copy, or `null`);
  `user_confirmation` (step 1's literal text, so the transaction's
  authority is itself durable and a recovery run needs no fresh
  confirmation to finish — or to undo — work the user already authorized);
  `approval_now`, `expected_post_state_b64`, and
  `expected_post_state_sha256` (all new, revision 56, `GPT-R73-002` — see
  immediately below); and `created_at`. A journal exists **if and only if**
  an approval
  transaction for this work item is in flight: it is opened at step 4a,
  before the first mutation of any kind, and closed at step 8a, after the
  last verification passes. Its presence is therefore the durable,
  fresh-session-visible signal that this work item is mid-transaction.
  It is deliberately a separate file rather than a new
  `docs/ai-workflow/WORKFLOW_STATE.json` field: the journal's whole purpose
  is to survive — and drive — the restoration of that exact file, so
  storing it inside the artifact it restores would be circular (the
  rollback's own first action would delete its own instructions). Keeping
  it out also means this fix requires no `WORKFLOW_STATE.json` schema
  change and therefore no `D3` validator change, which matters because
  `workflow-v2-1-core` is permanently `governing_workflow_version: "1"`
  and the state file it shares with other work items must stay readable by
  the unmodified v1 commands throughout.

  **Exact expected post-approval state, and the canonical serialization it
  requires (new, revision 56, `GPT-R73-002`)**: revision 55's journal bound
  only the transaction's *pre*-state. Everything downstream that needed to
  recognize the *post*-state — the rollback's "is this my own write?"
  predicate — therefore had to guess from two fields (`phase ==
  "IMPLEMENTING"` plus a matching `approved_review_content_id`), which is
  satisfied by infinitely many files, including this transaction's own
  write plus a legitimate concurrent update to a **different** work item.
  Independently reproduced against the bundled `apply_plan_approval` (see
  "WF8b finding disposition (revision 55 → 56)" below). The transaction
  therefore binds both ends:
  - `approval_now`: the single ISO-8601 timestamp this transaction will use
    as `apply_plan_approval(...)`'s `now` argument, **pinned once, here**.
    It is a recorded input rather than a value read from the clock at write
    time, because `apply_plan_approval` writes it into two fields
    (`plan_approval.recorded_at` via the record built in step 2, and
    `last_transition`); a value sampled later would make the post-state
    unpredictable and therefore unbindable, and would make a fresh-session
    forward completion produce different bytes from the ones the commit
    already carries.
  - `expected_post_state_b64`/`expected_post_state_sha256`: the exact bytes
    `apply_plan_approval(pre_state, "workflow-v2-1-core", <step 2's
    record>, approval_now)` serializes to, computed **here**, before any
    mutation, from the pre-state bytes this same journal records. Because
    that function is a pure `copy.deepcopy`-plus-field-assignment over the
    parsed pre-state (independently confirmed: byte-identical output for a
    fixed `now`), these bytes are fully determined at step 4a and every
    later check — staged blob, committed blob, working-tree
    materialization, fresh-session forward completion — compares against
    this one recorded identity rather than recomputing a fresh guess.
  - **Canonical serialization**: `json.dumps(state, indent=2,
    ensure_ascii=False) + "\n"`, UTF-8 encoded. This is stated normatively
    here because binding exact bytes is meaningless without it, and nothing
    in this repository stated it before: `scripts/workflow_state.py` has no
    `WORKFLOW_STATE.json` writer of its own (the state file is written by
    the commands, not the library), and neither `.claude/commands/` nor
    `docs/ai-workflow/REVIEW_PROTOCOL.md` names a serialization. Verified
    directly against this repository's own live
    `docs/ai-workflow/WORKFLOW_STATE.json`: this exact form round-trips it
    byte-identically, while the two obvious neighbours do not —
    `ensure_ascii=True` (the default) escapes the file's non-ASCII
    characters, and `sort_keys=True` reorders `work_items` entries. Any
    implementation of this procedure that serializes differently produces a
    post-state that fails its own binding check, which is the intended
    fail-closed outcome rather than a silent divergence.

    This rule constrains only what **this transaction writes**, not what it
    reads. The pre-state is captured as raw bytes and compared as raw bytes
    everywhere it is used (the journal digest, sub-step 6.1a's
    compare-and-swap, step 8b's first branch), so a pre-state file some
    other command happened to write with a different serialization is
    handled correctly: the transaction's own output is canonical, the
    commit and the materialized working-tree file are byte-identical to
    each other, and step 9's clean-tree confirmation holds. The only
    visible effect is that an approval commit may also normalize the file's
    formatting, which is harmless — `WORKFLOW_STATE.json` is plan-stage
    excluded, so it contributes to no `review_content_id`. Missing-test
    item 353 makes the canonical serialization an implementation-acceptance
    obligation for every command that writes this file, so the normalization
    happens once rather than oscillating between writers.

  **No usable partial approval state (new, revision 56, `GPT-R73-001` — the
  structural half of the fix)**: revision 55 left a real interval in which
  the working-tree `WORKFLOW_STATE.json` carried `status: CURRENT` /
  `phase: IMPLEMENTING` while no approval commit existed, and defended it
  with a *normative* rule ("while a journal exists, no other command may
  act on this work item's state") that the one command able to act —
  the installed `/bootstrap-workflow-v2` — does not implement and cannot be
  made to implement without editing `.claude/commands/`, which a plan-only
  revision does not do. A rule the currently-executable command surface
  ignores is not a lock.

  This revision removes the interval instead of guarding it. The
  transaction never writes the post-approval state into the **working
  tree** until a verified durable approval commit already exists; it stages
  the exact expected post-state bytes **directly into the Git index** as a
  blob (`git hash-object -w` followed by `git update-index --add
  --cacheinfo`), commits from that verified index, and only then
  materializes the file (step 8b). Independently reproduced in an isolated
  scratch repository: staging a blob this way leaves the working-tree file
  byte-unchanged, a pathspec-free `git commit` commits the pinned blob, and
  writing the file afterwards lands on a clean tree.

  The consequence is the enforcement property revision 55 could only
  assert. Throughout the entire vulnerable interval — journal open, index
  staged, commit attempted, commit rejected by step 7, or hard interruption
  at any point — the working-tree `plan_approval.approved_review_content_id`
  is still the **previous** approval's value. `/bootstrap-workflow-v2`'s
  step-2 durability guard recomputes the plan-stage `review_content_id` and
  compares it against exactly that field, so it observes a mismatch and
  stops, naming both values, precisely as it already does today. Confirmed
  against this repository's own live state: the guard's two inputs are
  currently `68eed7ec…` (recorded) versus `cb5e5ea4…` (recomputed), and it
  is revision 55's step-6 *working-tree* write that would have made them
  equal. `/milestone-implement`'s `implementing_entry_reachable(...)` route
  already failed closed and is unaffected. No command can therefore consume
  a partial `CURRENT`/`IMPLEMENTING` state, because no partial
  `CURRENT`/`IMPLEMENTING` state is ever written where a command would read
  it — and this holds without editing a single installed command file, and
  equally for the second shape the finding names (a durable commit that
  step 7 has already rejected, whose working-tree state is likewise still
  the previous approval's).

  This also dissolves the rollback's data-loss exposure at the root:
  see the rollback contract below.

  **Approval-transaction outcome classifier**: given a validated journal,
  decides what actually happened from durable Git state alone — never from
  a command's exit status, and never from `WORKFLOW_STATE.json`, which is
  exactly the artifact whose trustworthiness is in question. It has two
  entry points and one definition: step 6 calls it in-session immediately
  after its `git commit` attempt, and step 0 calls it on a fresh session
  after an interruption. Making both paths the same operation is
  deliberate — the crash-recovery path is then exercised by every ordinary
  in-session failure, not only after a real crash.
  1. Look up the durable approval commit with
     `workflow_state.discover_plan_approval_commit(repo_root,
     <the journal's work_item_id>, <the journal's
     expected_review_content_id>, <the journal's base_commit>,
     head="HEAD")` — `D-Commit-Provenance`'s scoped, ancestry-limited,
     exactly-one-match trailer lookup that every other durability check
     already uses, never an ad hoc `git log --grep`. Every argument comes
     from the validated journal or from live Git; none is read from
     `WORKFLOW_STATE.json`.
  2. **`COMMITTED`**: exactly one commit `C` matches, `C`'s first parent is
     exactly the journal's `pre_procedure_head`, and `C` is reachable from
     live `HEAD`. The transaction reached durability and `C` is its commit.
  3. **`NOT_COMMITTED`**: no commit matches **and** live `HEAD` is still
     exactly `pre_procedure_head`. Nothing durable was created.
  4. **`AMBIGUOUS`**: every other shape — a match whose first parent is not
     `pre_procedure_head`; no match while `HEAD` has moved off
     `pre_procedure_head`; or `AmbiguousApprovalTrailerError` raised by the
     lookup itself. The procedure refuses, mutates nothing further, leaves
     the journal in place, and reports both the observed and the expected
     shape for manual resolution. Neither rolling back (which could strand
     or contradict a real approval) nor completing forward (which could
     bless a commit this transaction did not create) is safe on an
     ambiguous shape, so neither is attempted.

  **Approval-transaction rollback**: the single automatic recovery for
  **every** failure occurring after the journal is opened and before the
  classifier returns `COMMITTED`. It runs only on a validated journal, only
  on a `NOT_COMMITTED` classification, and — new, revision 57,
  `GPT-R74-001` — **only when the session running it holds the journal's
  current `owner_token`**. Both of its mutating operations — the index reset
  (2) and the journal deletion (5) — run inside the transaction mutation
  guard, each under `step_class: "destructive"`, with `assert_owner` called
  **inside** that guard (revised, revision 58, `GPT-R75-001`; revision 57
  called `assert_owner` immediately *before* each, which is the same
  check-to-use shape `GPT-R75-001` found). A session that does not hold the
  token can therefore neither reset the index on a live owner's behalf nor
  remove that owner's recovery record, and — because a `"destructive"` guard
  is never breakable by any authorization — no takeover can rotate ownership
  out from under either operation once it has begun. So the rollback can
  never undo a durable approval, and it can no longer undo — or erase the
  undo record of — a transaction belonging to someone else.
  1. **Write no `WORKFLOW_STATE.json` bytes at all** (rewritten, revision
     56, `GPT-R73-002`). Revision 55's rollback restored the whole file
     from the journal's `pre_procedure_state_b64` whenever it *recognized*
     the current file, and recognized it from two fields: `phase ==
     "IMPLEMENTING"` and a matching `approved_review_content_id`. Both
     fields are equally true of this transaction's own write **and** of
     that same write plus a sanctioned concurrent update to a different
     work item — the exact case `D1` calls normal, since
     `active_work_item_id` is a resume-focus pointer, not an execution
     lock, and multiple non-terminal work items are expected.
     Independently reproduced against the bundled `apply_plan_approval`:
     the predicate accepts a state whose `milestone-8` entry has legitimately
     advanced, and restoring the whole pre-procedure file at that point
     necessarily deletes that other work item's update.

     Under revision 56's index-pinned state write there is nothing here to
     restore: the transaction never wrote the working-tree file. Rollback
     therefore **touches `docs/ai-workflow/WORKFLOW_STATE.json` not at
     all**, and the destroy-a-concurrent-writer branch is not narrowed or
     conditioned — it is removed, because the operation that could perform
     it no longer exists. What was a promise about restoration becomes a
     structural property: an approval transaction that fails before
     durability leaves the shared state file exactly as whoever last wrote
     it left it, whether that was this session or another work item's
     legitimate concurrent operation. `D1`'s multi-work-item concurrency
     model and this transaction's rollback are thereby reconciled by
     construction rather than by an unenforceable global write lock.

     What the rollback does assert about that file is one **read-only**
     safety check: the current file's `work_items["workflow-v2-1-core"]`
     must **not** carry `plan_approval.approved_review_content_id ==
     <the journal's expected_review_content_id>` with `phase ==
     "IMPLEMENTING"`. Under this design that combination is unreachable
     before a durable commit, so observing it means an implementation
     violated the index-pinned-write rule (or a third party wrote it).
     Refuse, leave the journal in place, and report — the transaction's own
     invariant is broken and blind repair would compound it. This is an
     assertion, never a repair, and it can never delete anyone's data.
  2. **Under the mutation guard** (`step: "rollback-index-reset"`,
     `step_class: "destructive"`, `assert_owner` run inside it, guard
     released after the progress record advances), restore the whole index
     to `HEAD` with an explicit `git reset --mixed
     HEAD` — the mode named literally, never a bare `git reset`, never
     `--soft` or `--hard`. This restores every index entry to `HEAD` and
     touches no working-tree file (independently reproduced; see "WF8b
     finding disposition (revision 54 → 55)" below). It lands exactly on
     the step-3 state, and it cannot destroy staged content the user
     owned, because step 3 already proved the index equal to `HEAD` before
     the journal was opened: there was none. This is also why the
     whole-index form is required here where a per-path `git restore
     --staged` list would not suffice — a failing `pre-commit` hook can
     leave paths staged that this procedure never named, and only a
     whole-index restore is guaranteed to catch them.
  3. Touch no working-tree file. The reviewed plan/registry/mapping/
     declaration edits survive verbatim, so a retry recomputes the
     identical `bundle_id`/`review_content_id` and re-enters the same
     external-review gate with nothing to reconstruct.
  4. **Verify the rollback before believing it**: require `git diff
     --cached --quiet` to report a clean index; require `git rev-parse
     HEAD` to still equal `pre_procedure_head`; and require the read-only
     assertion in (1) to hold — the working-tree state file does not carry
     this transaction's own post-approval identity. (Revised, revision 56:
     the former "`WORKFLOW_STATE.json` sha256 equals
     `pre_procedure_state_sha256`" check is deliberately **dropped**. It
     would now fail on exactly the legitimate case this revision exists to
     protect — another work item's concurrent write — and would convert a
     correct, data-preserving rollback into a permanent refusal. The
     transaction no longer writes that file, so it has no claim to make
     about its bytes.) If any check fails, the rollback did **not**
     complete: stop, report the exact failed check, and deliberately
     **leave the journal in place**, so a later fresh session re-enters
     step 0 with the recovery information intact rather than losing it.
  5. Only once every check in (4) passes, **acquire the mutation guard**
     (`step: "rollback-close-journal"`, `step_class: "destructive"`), run
     `assert_owner` inside it, and
     then delete the journal (`os.remove`, then `os.fsync` the containing
     directory), followed by the owner progress record
     (`PLAN_APPROVAL_OWNER.<owner_token>.json`) and any claim link for a
     token in `previous_owner_tokens`, and finally release the guard itself
     (`os.unlink`; `FileNotFoundError` is success) — the guard is released
     last, so no window exists in which the journal is gone but a takeover
     could still believe it may act (revision 58). **An already-absent journal is
     success, not an error** (revision 56, stress pass 2): a
     `FileNotFoundError` here means this same transaction was already
     resolved, which is the outcome this deletion was trying to reach.
     Treating it as a failure would turn a completed recovery into a
     reported one, so the deletion is idempotent — the same property step
     8a's deletion has, and for the same reason. Note the ordering
     (revision 57, tightened revision 58): `assert_owner` runs **inside the
     guard and before** the deletion, so an
     already-absent journal is only ever reached by the session that held
     the token; a non-owner fails the assertion and never reaches the
     deletion at all, and no takeover can rotate ownership while the
     deletion is in flight.
  6. Report the refusal and its concrete cause, state that the work item is
     back at `AWAITING_EXTERNAL_PLAN_REVIEW` with a clean index and an
     unmodified `WORKFLOW_STATE.json` (revised, revision 56: unmodified
     *by this transaction*, which is the stronger and now literally true
     statement — the transaction never wrote it), and stop. The retry is
     this procedure from the beginning (step 0), with no manual
     `WORKFLOW_STATE.json` or index
     repair of any kind.

  0. **Interrupted-transaction recovery precondition (new, revision 55,
     `GPT-R72-001`)**: before step 1, and before any other step, check
     whether `.ai-review/runtime/PLAN_APPROVAL_JOURNAL.json` exists.
     - **Absent**: no transaction is in flight; proceed to step 1. (An
       absent journal alongside a `CURRENT` `plan_approval` and a
       discoverable approval commit is the ordinary post-approval steady
       state.)
     - **Present**: a transaction exists that did not reach step 8a. Read
       the journal with an ordinary read — no lock (revision 57): under
       link-publication the final pathname only ever holds a complete
       inode, and the one in-place replacement (takeover) is atomic against
       readers, so there is no torn read to prevent.

       **Zero-length or unparseable journal — fail closed** (rewritten,
       revision 57, `GPT-R74-001`; **replaces** revision 56's
       "crashed-at-acquisition" auto-delete branch): revision 56 created
       the final pathname empty and populated it afterwards, so a
       zero-length journal was read as proof that the previous attempt died
       inside its own write. That inference was wrong, and the branch
       acting on it was the concrete defect: independently reproduced, a
       resolver took exactly this branch, confirmed a clean index, and
       deleted the journal of a **live** transaction that was still between
       its own `O_EXCL` creation and its own write — after which the owner
       wrote and `fsync`ed an unlinked inode and continued, believing
       publication had succeeded, with no journal anywhere. Under revision
       57's link-publication the final pathname can no longer hold an
       incomplete journal at all, so this shape can only mean the journal
       was corrupted by something outside this procedure or written by an
       implementation that violated the publication contract. Neither is
       something a resolver may repair by deletion: **refuse, mutate
       nothing, delete nothing, leave the journal in place, and report**
       the exact defect for manual resolution. A stray
       `.ai-review/runtime/` temporary file from an interrupted publication
       is *not* this shape and is never acted on — it does not occupy the
       final pathname.

       Otherwise validate the journal: require `schema_version == 3`
       (revision 58) and every
       field the journal contract names; require `stage == "plan"` and
       `work_item_id == "workflow-v2-1-core"`; require
       `sha256(b64decode(pre_procedure_state_b64)) ==
       pre_procedure_state_sha256`; require
       `sha256(b64decode(expected_post_state_b64)) ==
       expected_post_state_sha256` (new, revision 56); require
       `expected_post_state_b64` to decode to valid JSON whose
       `work_items["workflow-v2-1-core"]` carries `phase == "IMPLEMENTING"`
       and `plan_approval.approved_review_content_id ==
       expected_review_content_id` (new, revision 56 — the recorded
       post-state must actually *be* an approval of the round this journal
       names, so a well-formed but wrong post-state cannot be blessed by a
       later forward completion); and require the recorded
       `repo_root`/`git_common_dir`/`worktree_root` triple to equal this
       worktree's own; and — new, revision 57 — require `owner_token` to be
       exactly 32 lowercase hex characters, `takeover_count` to be a
       non-negative integer equal to `len(previous_owner_tokens)`, and
       `previous_owner_tokens` to be a list of distinct 32-hex tokens none
       of which equals the current `owner_token`; and — new, revision 58,
       `GPT-R75-002` — require `quiescence_authorization` to be a non-empty
       string naming `workflow-v2-1-core` and the `plan` stage, since a
       journal that cannot show the window's authority must never reach the
       materialization step that depends on it. Any failure — a
       parseable but schema-invalid
       journal, a missing field, either digest mismatch, a malformed
       ownership field, a missing or malformed quiescence authorization,
       another work item,
       or another worktree — refuses
       outright, mutates nothing at all, and reports the exact defect for
       manual resolution: a journal this session cannot fully authenticate
       is never acted on.

       **Then check ownership before resolving anything** (new, revision
       57, `GPT-R74-001`). A validated journal is *not* by itself an
       invitation to resolve it:
       - **This session holds the journal's current `owner_token`** — it
         published this journal, or took it over earlier — so it is the
         owner. Run the outcome classifier and act on its single answer:
         - `COMMITTED`: the approval commit is durable. Complete
           **forward** — run steps 7, 8, 8b, 8a, and 9 against that commit,
           exactly as an uninterrupted run would. Never roll back.
         - `NOT_COMMITTED`: run the approval-transaction rollback, then
           stop.
         - `AMBIGUOUS`: refuse, mutate nothing, leave the journal in place,
           and report.
       - **This session does not hold it** — the ordinary fresh-session
         case — so it is **not** the owner: **refuse by default.** Do not
         roll back, do not complete forward, do not replace the journal,
         and above all do not delete it. Report the journal's identity and
         `owner_token`, the owner progress record's `step_seq`/`updated_at`
         (or its absence), the **read-only** outcome classification
         (computing it mutates nothing, and it is exactly the evidence the
         user needs), and the two available resolutions: resume in the
         owning session, or take over explicitly. This is `GPT-R74-001`'s
         required correction (4), and it is what closes the interleaving
         revision 56 left open — a second session validating a live,
         fully-published, `NOT_COMMITTED` journal, running a rollback that
         is a verified no-op precisely *because* the owner had not staged
         anything yet, and deleting that owner's only recovery record.
       - **Explicit takeover**: when, and only when, the user supplies the
         literal takeover confirmation the "Refuse by default; takeover is
         explicit" contract above defines, perform that contract's
         claim/re-verify/rotate sequence. On success this session holds the
         rotated `owner_token` and continues at the owner branch above,
         with the same classifier and the same forward/rollback logic —
         required correction (5). On any refusal within that sequence —
         claim lost, `owner_token` advanced, progress advanced — nothing
         has been mutated and the live owner is untouched.

       **This ownership rule governs every "a fresh session re-enters step
       0" statement in this procedure** (new, revision 57 — stated once
       here rather than repeated at each site, and load-bearing wherever
       steps 7, 8, 8a, 8b and 10 describe fresh-session resumption). Those
       statements describe what step 0 *decides*, not an entitlement to
       skip it: a session re-entering step 0 resolves the transaction only
       if it already holds the journal's `owner_token`, and otherwise
       refuses until an explicit takeover grants it one. No resumption
       path anywhere in this procedure bypasses that check. The stray
       `PLAN_APPROVAL_OWNER.<token>.json` and
       `PLAN_APPROVAL_JOURNAL.claim.<token>` files a previous transaction
       may leave behind are inert for the same reason a stray publication
       temporary is: they are gitignored, they are never at the journal's
       pathname, and no step reads a file whose embedded token is not the
       journal's current or superseded one.
     - **While a journal exists, this work item is mid-transaction**, and
       no other command may act on `workflow-v2-1-core`'s state until
       step 0 has resolved it — not `/bootstrap-workflow-v2`, not
       `/milestone-implement`, not bundle generation, not a second
       concurrent run of this procedure.

       **How that rule is actually enforced, per addressee (rewritten,
       revision 56, `GPT-R73-001`)**. Revision 55 stated this rule
       normatively and deferred its only enforcement to missing-test item
       352 — that is, to implementation work scheduled *after* the very
       approval this bridge exists to make safe. A rule whose enforcement
       arrives after the event it guards is not a lock, and the installed
       `/bootstrap-workflow-v2` command reads no journal. The rule is
       therefore now backed by three concrete mechanisms, each covering a
       distinct addressee, all effective **before** this revision's own
       approval is attempted:
       1. **A second run of this procedure** — the atomic, no-replace
          `os.link` publication of the journal (revision 57; revision 56's
          `O_CREAT | O_EXCL` creation). The second run's publication fails
          outright and it refuses, having mutated nothing. Exclusive by
          construction, not by convention.
       1a. **A second *recovery* session** (new, revision 57,
          `GPT-R74-001`) — the durable `owner_token`. A session that does
          not hold it refuses at step 0 rather than rolling back,
          completing forward, or deleting the journal, and every mutating
          step of the owning transaction re-asserts the token before it
          runs. Exclusivity of *creation* was never exclusivity of
          *ownership*; this is the mechanism that supplies the latter.
       2. **The installed `/bootstrap-workflow-v2`, and any other command
          that reads approval state** — the index-pinned state write ("No
          usable partial approval state" above). There is no interval in
          which the working-tree `WORKFLOW_STATE.json` carries a `CURRENT`
          plan approval for this round without a durable approval commit,
          so that command's own existing step-2 durability guard already
          refuses throughout the transaction, unchanged and unaware of the
          journal. The same holds for the second shape this rule must
          cover — a durable commit that step 7 rejected — since the
          working-tree state file is likewise still the previous
          approval's. `/milestone-implement`'s
          `workflow_state.implementing_entry_reachable(...)` route
          independently fails closed, as it already did, by requiring a
          discoverable approval commit reachable from `HEAD`.
       2a. **Every other installed command that writes
          `docs/ai-workflow/WORKFLOW_STATE.json`** (new, revision 58,
          `GPT-R75-002`) — the temporary state-writer quiescence window,
          required at step 4a and defined at step 8b. Mechanism (2) is
          structural but *narrow*: it stops a command from **consuming a
          partial approval** for this work item; it does nothing to stop one
          from **writing a different work item's entry** into the same
          shared file, which is what `GPT-R75-002`'s lost update actually
          was. Nothing in the currently installed surface prevents that, so
          the rule is carried by an explicit user authorization with a
          durable journal record, an exhaustive prohibited-writer list, and
          a stated violation behavior — not by a claim that concurrent
          writers are harmless. It is temporary by construction and retired
          by (4).
       3. **The permanent fix for the approval-consumption half** —
          missing-test item 352 still binds
          `/bootstrap-workflow-v2`'s step-2 guard to a *discovered durable
          approval commit* rather than to
          `plan_approval.approved_review_content_id`, and adds an explicit
          journal precondition. That remains the right end state and is
          strictly stronger than (2); it is no longer this contract's only
          line of defence, and no longer the one that has to land first.
       4. **The permanent fix for the shared-write half** (new, revision 58;
          retirement condition and consumer stated exactly, revision 61,
          `GPT-R78-001`/`-002`)
          — missing-test item 354, now owned by `WF8b`'s continued scope
          (`GPT-R75-003`), makes every supported writer acquire
          `.ai-review/runtime/WORKFLOW_STATE.lock`, at which point the lock
          becomes the mechanism. (2a) is then retired **for item 347's
          permanent `/approve-review`, and only there** — never for this
          temporary bridge, which requires the authorization on every run
          — and only once that landing has itself been independently
          reviewed and technically approved and the gate *derives* `PASS`
          for `WFO-STATE-SERIALIZATION` through the approved verifier
          (`D-Completion-Obligations`). Until all of that holds, the lock is
          not the mechanism and (2a) stands.
       The distinction matters because (2) and (2a) are the only ones true
       of the command surface a user can invoke **today**,
       with no file under `.claude/commands/` or `scripts/` edited — which
       is exactly the constraint this bridge operates under — and because
       they cover different halves of the problem: (2) is mechanical and
       narrow, (2a) is broad and authorization-based. Neither is a
       substitute for the other, and this revision does not present either
       as more than it is.
  1. **User-only guard, preserved**: this procedure performs the identical
     class of state/commit writes `/approve-review plan` itself performs,
     so it is gated identically — Claude never performs any step below
     absent the user's own current-turn literal confirmation text naming
     `workflow-v2-1-core` and `plan` (the same text `/approve-review`'s
     own mechanism (2) requires). The user does not separately invoke
     `/approve-review plan workflow-v2-1-core` for a round this procedure
     covers; giving this same confirmation text is itself the trigger for
     this procedure instead.
  2. **Steps 1-4 of `/approve-review`, unchanged, performed directly,
     read-only (reordered, revision 52, `GPT-R69-001`)**: confirm gate
     reachability (`workflow_state.approval_gate_reachable`); recompute
     `bundle_id`/plan-stage `review_content_id` fresh and run the local
     worktree/HEAD staleness check
     (`workflow_fingerprint.assert_local_generation_matches`); **assert the
     recomputed plan-stage `review_content_id` equals the reviewed content
     identity** and refuse, naming both digests, on a difference (new,
     revision 75, `OPUS-R92-001` — the "Approval-time reviewed-identity
     freshness" bullet above, inherited here rather than restated, since this
     step is defined as `/approve-review`'s own steps 1-4). **The reviewed
     value's source, in this interval, is the bullet's "The bridge interval,
     and it expires" clause and it must be read before this step is executed**
     (new, revision 76, `OPUS-R93-001`): this procedure has no code — item 348
     states it is exercised as a live checklist, so its execution surface is
     this document — and the corroborating source the permanent rule names,
     `parse_review_feedback_binding_fields`' fourth binding field, does **not
     exist yet**. A session that reaches this step and calls that parser gets a
     dict with no reviewed-content key and has no sanctioned next move; the
     three unsanctioned ones are all bad, and the worst of them (treat the
     assertion as unimplemented and fall through to steps 3-4) reproduces
     exactly the `EXTERNAL_APPROVE`-on-drifted-content defect this revision's
     predecessor exists to remove. So: read the identity from
     `read_manifest_identifiers(<bundle_dir>/MANIFEST.md)["review_content_id"]`,
     corroborate it against the feedback's `Reviewed review content ID:` line
     read directly, and compare both against a freshly recomputed
     `compute_review_content_id_plan_stage_for_work_item(...)`. All three are
     read-only and all three ship today. Resolve the
     basis (`workflow_state.resolve_approval_basis`); build the record
     (`workflow_state.build_approval_record`). None of these steps
     reference the commit's file set, so none of them differ from an
     ordinary `/approve-review plan` run — and, unlike revision 51, none of

        working-tree bytes for the named paths rather than committing the
        already-verified, pinned index blob — silently bypassing the
        fifth-member pin if the working tree changed again after step 5.

        cannot be bypassed this way.

        after it reported an error," and rolling back on the second of

        defect this whole step exists to fix.

          refuse, quoting Git's own error output. This is the branch that
          covers a failing `pre-commit`/`commit-msg` hook, a commit-signing
          failure, a filesystem or Git error, and any other ordinary local
          commit failure. All of these were independently reproduced

  8b. **Materialize the post-approval state in the working tree (new,

      index pin, and the **only** point at which this procedure writes

      durable approval commit exists and has passed step 7's committed
