is `(C, obligation_content_id)`; `verifier_identity` is defined in the next
subsection. Both are immutable, and both are recorded, so a recorded verdict
keeps its meaning no matter what later implementation history does — which is
`GPT-R78-001`'s required corrections (5) and (6). Every Git read is issued with `--no-replace-objects` and
`GIT_NO_REPLACE_OBJECTS=1` (revision 60, stress pass 3): `git replace` refs
rewrite what an object id resolves to and would otherwise break exactly the
content-addressing this design rests on — reproduced both ways, including the
dangerous direction of substituting honest bytes over a failing blob, which the
hardened reader refuses.

**Freshness binds the discovered writer *set*, not a remembered list**
(revision 60, resolves `GPT-R77-002`). `obligation_content_id` is a sha256 over
a canonical JSON projection containing: the obligation id; the **surface
definitions** themselves; the **complete surface census** — an ordered
`{path, blob}` entry for *every* tracked file on a declared surface, not merely
the ones that turned out to be writers; the declared writer subset; the declared
publisher set; the serialization helper's blob; and the conformance
implementation's blob. Revision 59 hashed "the twelve state-writing command
files," which `GPT-R77-002` correctly showed leaves writer-set *membership*
outside the identity — reproduced: adding a thirteenth unlocked state-writing
command left the digest bit-for-bit identical and the prior `PASS` current.
Because the census is the whole surface rather than the writer subset, adding a
file to a surface changes the identity even when that file declares nothing at
all — a gap found and closed by this revision's own stress pass 1, which
initially bound only the writer subset and watched an undeclared thirteenth
command leave the identity unchanged.

Since the verdict is re-derived on every evaluation, staleness is not a state
the mechanism can be in: there is no `STALE` classification any more, because
`STALE` was a property of a cached record. The identity is retained for
**audit and binding**, not for cache validation.

**The verifier is authorized by the workflow's existing implementation-stage
technical approval — it does not authorize itself** (new, revision 61, resolves
`GPT-R78-001`). Revision 60 pinned *what is checked* to immutable Git objects
and left *who checks it* as arbitrary live `HEAD`. `GPT-R78-001` found the
consequence and this revision reproduced it before accepting anything: with a
converted repository and a legitimate prior approval, one unreviewed commit that
changed a state writer **and** rebound `WFO-STATE-SERIALIZATION` to an
unconditional-`PASS` conformance produced `PASS` under revision 60's contract,
with the working tree clean and equal to that `HEAD` so the divergence
precondition stayed silent. The same held for a discovery changed to omit the
writer it had just broken. The plan's own sentence — "the binding from obligation
id to conformance lives in the implementation rather than the registry, so it is
covered by implementation-stage review" — was true of what *review* covers and
false of what the *gate* required, because the gate consulted no approval at all.

Two identities are therefore named separately and never conflated:

- **Subject identity** — `(C, obligation_content_id)`: the exact immutable
  content whose serialization invariant is being evaluated (the surface
  definitions, the complete surface census, the discovered writer set, the
  publisher and the helper, all read from Git objects at `C`).
- **Verifier identity** — `(verifier_identity_id, verifier_census)`: the exact
  independently reviewed implementation of discovery, projection, conformance
  and verdict derivation that is authorized to judge that subject. The
  `verifier_census` is an ordered `{path, mode, blob, source}` list over the
  **execution-complete repository-local dependency closure** of the declared
  verifier entry point — **not** a hand-written file list (**corrected,
  revision 62, `GPT-R79-002`**; see "The verifier census is a dependency
  closure" below) — and `verifier_identity_id` is a sha256 over the canonical
  JSON of `{verifier_entry, verifier_source_root, verifier_census}`.

**No second approval system is created — but authority comes from the durable
approval *commit*, not from the mutable record** (rewritten, revision 62,
resolves `GPT-R79-001`). The authority is still the one the workflow already
uses for exactly this content class: `.claude/commands/` and `scripts/` are both
implementation-stage **protected prefixes** in this work item's own
`<work_item_id>-artifacts.json`, so the state writers, the discovery, the
binding and the conformance are already the content `technical_approval` binds
to. What revision 61 got wrong is *where the record is read from*. It specified
`approval_is_current(..., stage="implementation", head=C)` as the whole
authority resolution, and `GPT-R79-001` correctly found that this predicate
proves **freshness only**. Confirmed against the bundled implementation before
anything was changed — `approval_is_current` (`scripts/workflow_state.py:934-960`)
reads `work_item["technical_approval"]`, requires `status == "CURRENT"`,
recomputes the stage identity at `head` and compares the two digests. It never
calls `discover_technical_approval_commit(...)` (`:839-846`), never requires a
reachable trailer commit, never checks ancestry, and never compares the live
record against anything committed. `WORKFLOW_STATE.json` is intentionally
runtime-mutable and implementation-stage **excluded**, so this is the same shape
this plan already rejected twice: a self-authored local record standing in for an
independent event. The repository already contains the missing primitive — the
same `Workflow-Technical-Approval`/`Workflow-Work-Item` trailer discovery
`implementing_entry_reachable` (`:963-984`) already uses for the *plan* stage.
Revision 61's gate simply did not consume it. **Revision 62 consumes it, and
invents nothing.**

`resolve_completion_obligations(...)` resolves authority in this exact order,
for the work item that **owns** the obligation:

1. **Recompute the implementation-stage identity at the pinned subject `C`** —
   `approval_review_content_id(..., stage="implementation", head=C)`, at the
   same pinned commit the subject is read from, never a second live `HEAD` read.
   Any failure to evaluate it at all (`UnclassifiedPathError` above all)
   classifies `VERIFIER_UNRESOLVABLE`.
2. **Discover the durable approval commit for *that recomputed identity*** —
   `discover_technical_approval_commit(repo_root, owner_id, <the recomputed id>,
   base_commit, C)`. The search key is the identity the gate just computed from
   committed content; **it is never a field of any record**, which is what makes
   a fabricated record irrelevant rather than merely insufficient. Genuine
   ambiguity (`AmbiguousApprovalTrailerError`, more than one first-parent-ancestor
   match after the existing tie-break) is caught and classified
   `VERIFIER_UNAPPROVED` — a refusal, never an escaping exception and never a
   silent pick.
3. **Require reachability**: no match, or a match that is not an ancestor of `C`
   (`_is_ancestor`), classifies `VERIFIER_UNAPPROVED`. A trailer commit that
   exists only on a foreign branch is outside `base_commit..C` and is therefore
   never found in the first place.
4. **Read the authoritative record out of the state file *that commit
   committed*** — `git cat-file blob <A>:docs/ai-workflow/WORKFLOW_STATE.json`,
   under the same `--no-replace-objects`/`GIT_NO_REPLACE_OBJECTS=1` hardening as
   every other object read here — and take
   `work_items[<owner_id>].technical_approval` from it. An unreadable or
   malformed committed state file, or one committing no record for the owner,
   classifies `VERIFIER_UNAPPROVED`.
5. **Validate that durable record on its own terms**: `status == "CURRENT"`; its
   `approved_review_content_id` equal to the identity recomputed in (1); a
   well-formed 40-hex `reviewed_content_commit`; a non-empty
   `review_content_manifest`.
6. **Require the live copy to agree, or refuse.** The live
   `WORKFLOW_STATE.json` record may still exist for runtime state, but it is
   never independently authority-bearing. Every authority-bearing field —
   `status`, `basis`, `approved_review_content_id`, `review_content_manifest`,
   `reviewed_content_commit`, `reviewed_bundle_id`, `user_confirmation`,
   `legacy_evidence`, `waived_guarantees` — must equal the durable record's.
   A mismatch **refuses, naming the diverging fields**; it never silently
   chooses a side. An absent live record refuses too.
6b. **Require the live `base_commit` to equal the one the approval commit
   committed** (revision 62, stress pass 3, `R62-S3-002`). `base_commit` is
   folded into the implementation-stage projection, so leaving it a live mutable
   input would leave one authority-bearing digest input outside the durable
   record's reach. It is pinned to the durable side like everything else.
7. **Build the verifier census** from the durable record (next subsection), and
   prove the verifier content at `C` equals the approved blobs, per path.
8. **Materialize and execute the verifier from those blobs** — the same
   `git cat-file`-into-a-scratch-directory mechanism revision 60 already uses
   for the serialization helper, applied to the checker itself, under the
   isolation contract the next subsection defines.
9. Derive the verdict, and accept `PASS` only if every relationship above held.

Because the implementation-stage projection hashes protected *content* and never
folds the commit id in, step (1)'s recomputation says exactly the right thing: it
is the identity of the protected implementation content at `C`. An unreviewed
change to `scripts/workflow_state.py`, to `scripts/workflow_fingerprint.py`, to
the obligation-to-conformance binding, to discovery, or to any state-writer
command changes it, so no approval commit carries it and the gate refuses; a
commit touching only implementation-stage **excluded** paths —
`docs/ai-workflow/WORKFLOW_STATE.json`, this plan document, the registry and
requirements artifacts, product-milestone narrative — leaves it unchanged, so
the metadata and provenance-permitted commits the existing rules already allow
create no false staleness and the durable approval stays usable. All of that was
verified rather than argued: see the revision-62 stress-pass table.

**What forging now costs, stated without euphemism.** This remains a
review-authority boundary, not a cryptographic one — see "What this does and
does not establish" below, which revision 62 does not weaken. What changed is
the *kind* of artifact a forgery requires. Under revision 61 it required an
edit to a runtime-mutable, implementation-stage-**excluded** local file that no
gate reads for provenance. Under revision 62 it requires a **durable commit, on
the first-parent ancestry path to `C`, carrying an exact trailer pair, whose own
committed state file contains a record agreeing with the live one on every
authority-bearing field** — the identical standard the workflow already applies
to plan approval, and an artifact that shows up in `git log` rather than in an
untracked working-tree edit. This plan does not claim that makes forgery
impossible; it claims, and demonstrates, that a fabricated record alone no
longer authorizes anything.

**Two new fail-closed classifications** join the existing set (refusal list
extended for durable provenance, revision 62, `GPT-R79-001`):
`VERIFIER_UNAPPROVED` — **no reachable `Workflow-Technical-Approval` commit
carries the identity recomputed at `C`**; a discovered approval commit that is
not an ancestor of `C`; **genuinely ambiguous** approval commits for that
identity; an approval commit whose committed `WORKFLOW_STATE.json` is
unreadable, malformed, or commits no record for the obligation's owner; a
durable record whose `status != "CURRENT"`, whose `approved_review_content_id`
is not the recomputed identity, whose `reviewed_content_commit` is null or
malformed, or whose `review_content_manifest` is empty; an **absent live record,
or a live record diverging from the durable one on any authority-bearing
field**; a live `base_commit` that is not the one the approval commit committed;
a derived verifier closure that is empty; a verifier dependency absent at `C`;
a verifier blob at `C` that is not the approved one; or a verifier dependency
outside the approved manifest that has changed since `base_commit`. And
`VERIFIER_UNRESOLVABLE` — the currency evaluation itself could not complete (an
`UnclassifiedPathError`, an unreadable object, any Git failure), or the verifier
contains a dynamic-import construct static closure cannot follow. Neither
satisfies; both refuse. `UnclassifiedPathError` in particular is a **refusal,
never an escaping exception**, and it is not hypothetical: against this
repository today `approval_is_current(stage="implementation")` raises it, for
`docs/ai-workflow/dry-run/` **and for `docs/improvements/`** — two prefixes the
plan stage classifies and the implementation stage does not (**scope corrected,
revision 62**: revision 61 recorded only the first, and enumerating all 85 paths
changed in `base_commit..HEAD` against the live declaration found four
unclassified files across those two prefixes). Item 359 owns closing that
asymmetry; until it is closed the honest answer for this repository is
`VERIFIER_UNRESOLVABLE`, and the gate says so instead of crashing — reproduced
against the live repository through the revision-62 authority chain itself, not
asserted (stress pass 3, C4).

**The verifier census is a dependency closure, not a file list** (new, revision
62, resolves `GPT-R79-002`). Revision 61 declared the verifier path set to be
"today `scripts/workflow_state.py`" and claimed the gate and replay "materialize
and execute the verifier from the approved blobs". That claim was false at that
path set, and the finding was reproduced exactly before being accepted:
`scripts/workflow_state.py:107` executes `import workflow_fingerprint as
fingerprint` at module import time, so copying only that blob into a scratch
directory and importing it with the live repository off the module search path
fails immediately with `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named
'workflow_fingerprint'`. Every way past that under revision 61's contract is
wrong in a different direction: importing the live helper makes the "approved
verifier" partly unreviewed; materializing it from the subject commit makes the
checker depend on a blob outside `verifier_identity`; and materializing it from
the full approval manifest still leaves historical replay unreconstructable from
the recorded census, because the dependency is in neither the census nor the
identity. `workflow_fingerprint.py` is not an incidental import — it implements
the classification and fingerprint operations `workflow_state.py` uses for
approval freshness and review identities, which is to say it is load-bearing for
the very authority resolution above.

**The fix is a closure, defined once and derived mechanically**, because
`GPT-R79-002` is explicit that patching today's list to two hard-coded filenames
is not acceptable unless the plan also defines how future dependency changes are
detected. The verifier identity is declared as:

- a **verifier entry point** — today `scripts/workflow_state.py`, the module
  holding `discover_state_writers`, the obligation-to-conformance binding, the
  projection and `derive_obligation_verdict`; and
- a **verifier source root** — today `scripts/`, the tracked tree the closure may
  draw repository-local dependencies from.

Both are declared constants of the implementation, never caller parameters
(item 358(e)). From them the census is **derived**, not maintained:

1. **Static import closure over the pinned blobs.** Starting at the entry point,
   each module's bytes are read *from Git objects at `C`* (never the working
   tree) and parsed with the standard library's `ast`. Every `import X` /
   `from X import …` anywhere in the tree — module level, function bodies,
   class bodies, `try:` blocks — is collected, and any name that resolves to a
   tracked module or package on the verifier source root is followed
   transitively. Parsing the whole AST rather than the module header is what
   makes a **lazily imported** dependency part of the census; reproduced
   directly (revision-62 stress pass 2, B1).
2. **Packages are followed as packages.** A name resolving to
   `<root>/<pkg>/__init__.py` contributes that package's entire tracked `.py`
   subtree, and materialization reproduces the directory layout, so submodule
   imports resolve. Today's verifier is flat and this changes nothing about it;
   it is specified so the contract generalizes rather than silently
   under-covering the first package a future revision adds (stress pass 2, B4).
3. **Constructs static closure cannot follow fail closed.** `importlib.import_module(...)`,
   bare `__import__(...)`, `exec(...)` and relative imports are detected and
   classify `VERIFIER_UNRESOLVABLE` — the verifier is refused rather than
   censused optimistically. Today's two modules contain none of them, which is
   a checked observation, not an assumption (stress pass 2, B2/B2b/B3).
4. **Each closure path is bound to the durable approved identity.** Where the
   durable `review_content_manifest` covers the path, the blob at `C` must equal
   the approved blob or the gate refuses, naming the file. Where it does not,
   the path is **provably unchanged since `base_commit`** — the
   implementation-stage manifest covers only paths changed in `base..commit`, so
   a dependency untouched since `base_commit` is legitimately absent from it —
   and that is **asserted rather than inferred**: `blob(C)` must equal
   `blob(base_commit)`, else refuse. Each census entry records which of the two
   sources bound it. This clause exists because its absence was a real defect:
   revision 62's own first draft required manifest coverage unconditionally and
   was reproduced permanently refusing a repository whose fingerprint helper had
   simply not changed since `base_commit` (`R62-S3-001`) — the same
   false-refusal shape as revision 61's `R61-S3-001`.
5. **`verifier_identity_id` is a sha256 over the canonical JSON of
   `{verifier_entry, verifier_source_root, verifier_census}`** — over the whole
   closure, and still deliberately **not** over `approved_review_content_id`
   (revision 61, stress pass 1, unchanged). Changing any executable
   repository-local verifier dependency rotates it; changing only a *writer*
   leaves it byte-identical. Both directions are asserted, not just the first.

**Isolated execution is what makes the closure's completeness a checked property
rather than an assumption.** Static analysis alone can be wrong; the runtime
contract catches it. The census is materialized into a scratch module tree
preserving import layout, and the verifier is executed in a **fresh interpreter
process** — never in-process, so a module already in `sys.modules` cannot mask a
missing dependency — launched with Python's isolated mode (`-I`, which ignores
`PYTHONPATH` and user site directories), no bytecode writing (`-B`), no site
processing (`-S`), and `sys.path` reset to the scratch module directory plus the
standard library alone. **The live repository is not a module source.** A
dependency missing from the census therefore raises `ModuleNotFoundError` and
fails closed; it cannot silently resolve against live code. Reproduced in both
directions, including with `PYTHONPATH` pointed deliberately at the live
`scripts/` directory, where the recorded dependency still wins and an omitted one
still fails (stress pass 2, B6/B7; `GPT-R79-002` reproduction 2/2b/3b).

The invariant the whole subsection exists to establish, stated plainly: **the
verifier executes successfully given only its recorded approved census, the
immutable subject Git objects, and the Python standard library — with the live
repository unavailable as an executable dependency source.** For today's
implementation the derived closure is exactly
`scripts/workflow_fingerprint.py` and `scripts/workflow_state.py`, which is a
recorded observation of this repository, never an input and never a hard-coded
pair.

**Authority is resolved per declared obligation, and from the obligation's
owner** (revision 61, stress pass 3). It is deliberately *not* a blanket
precondition on the work item being completed: a work item that declares no
obligation is vacuously satisfied and its `technical_approval` is never
consulted at all. Specifying it the other way round was reproduced making every
`LEGACY_V1` import permanently uncompletable — a `LEGACY_V1` record carries a
null `review_content_manifest` by design (`D2`), and `D-Legacy`'s imported
Milestone-8 entry declares no obligation, so demanding a verifier identity of it
would have been a false refusal in a mechanism that does not apply to it.
Symmetrically, the verifier authority for `WFO-STATE-SERIALIZATION` is always
`workflow-v2-1-core`'s own `technical_approval`, because that is the work item
that owns the obligation — approving some *other* work item's plan never
requires *that* item to have a technical approval of its own.

**What this does and does not establish, stated without euphemism.** This is a
review-authority boundary, not a cryptographic one, and the plan says so rather
than overclaiming the way revision 59 did about digests and revision 60 did
about replay. A process that is itself running unreviewed code can decline to
perform any of these checks; no design executed by the thing it distrusts can
prevent that, and this repository has no signing boundary to appeal to. What the
contract does establish is exactly what `GPT-R78-001` and `GPT-R79-001`/`-002`
ask for and is
mechanically checkable: the specified implementation refuses to let an
unreviewed change to the checker or to the checked content produce a
load-bearing `PASS`; **a self-authored runtime record with no durable approval
commit behind it authorizes nothing** (revision 62); the specification is itself
implementation-stage-reviewed
content (items 356/358/360/361 assert the behaviour, not the prose); the
verifier that
runs is materialized from its **complete** approved dependency closure and
executed with the live repository off the module path, rather than from the live
import; and
the recorded verifier identity lets a later auditor re-execute the exact
authorizing version and detect a discrepancy. "The working tree equals `HEAD`"
proves the installed bytes are the committed bytes and nothing more — it never
implies `HEAD` was reviewed, and no rule in this plan reads it that way.

**One live writer-set discovery implementation, feeding both consumers**
(revision 60, `GPT-R77-002`'s required correction (1)/(5)).
`discover_state_writers(repo_root, commit) -> Discovery` is the **only**
inventory of state writers anywhere in the system. Its return value is
simultaneously (i) the set the conformance validates and (ii) the projection
hashed into `obligation_content_id`, so the two cannot drift the way the 8-vs-12
prose list once did. This plan's twelve names become a *recorded observation of
today's repository*, never an input.

- **Surfaces are declared, recursive, and extension-agnostic.** Today:
  `.claude/commands/**` and `scripts/**` excluding `*_test.py`. Recursive
  because Claude Code installs namespaced commands as
  `.claude/commands/<ns>/<name>.md`, and a one-directory-level rule left that
  entire shape undiscovered — found by this revision's stress pass 2, where a
  namespaced unlocked writer was added and the gate still returned `PASS`.
  Extension-agnostic because a rule keyed on `.md`/`.py`/`.sh` is escapable by
  naming the file `.markdown` or `.bash` — found by stress pass 3, where both
  probes passed a surface keyed on extensions and both refuse under the widened
  one. `*_test.py` is excluded deliberately and the reason is stated rather than
  left implicit: test modules construct fixture state files in temporary roots
  by design, so including them would make every unrelated test edit a false
  staleness event, and the *exploit* path is closed elsewhere — a command that
  delegates its state write to a test module fails the routing check, which is
  asserted directly (item 357).
- **Every file on a surface must declare itself**, and the declaration is
  cross-checked rather than trusted: `state_writer: true` (a writer, which must
  route its write through the single publisher and must perform no direct write
  of the state path), `state_writer: false` (a non-writer, which must then not
  reference the state path or the publisher at all), or `state_writer:
  "publisher"` (exactly one file, which must be the serialization helper the
  projection names). A **missing or contradictory declaration is a conformance
  failure**, never a default — which is what makes adding a thirteenth command
  fail closed whether or not its author knew the rule existed.

**Three helpers, and exactly one predicate.** In `scripts/workflow_state.py`:

- `resolve_completion_obligations(repo_root, work_item) ->
  dict[str, ObligationVerdict]` — **note the signature: there is no `registry`
  parameter, no `evidence` parameter, and (revision 60) no `commit`
  parameter.** All three are resolved internally from `repo_root` and the work
  item's own declared `registry_path`/`work_item_id`, through the *same*
  authoritative resolution
  `resolve_own_registry_completion_status` already performs — safe-path
  validation, existence, JSON-object parsing, self-declared-`work_item_id`
  agreement, and `_assert_registry_covered_by_current_plan_approval`. A first
  draft of this section took a caller-supplied `registry` dict, which is
  precisely the trust boundary `GPT-R37-001` removed from `complete_work_item`
  one layer up: a caller could hand in a registry declaring no obligations at
  all and satisfy the gate vacuously, exactly as it could once hand in a
  registry declaring every checkpoint complete. The rule this plan already
  adopted for that defect applies unchanged here — **remove the trust boundary
  rather than tighten a check on it**. The same rule is why revision 60 removes
  the `commit` parameter a first draft of this section gave it: stress pass 2
  handed the gate an *ancestor* commit at which the conformance had passed while
  `HEAD` genuinely failed, restored the working tree to that ancestor's content
  so the divergence precondition stayed silent, and watched the gate return
  `PASS`. A caller-supplied identity is a caller-supplied verdict. The gate
  resolves `HEAD` itself; a caller that pinned an identity earlier passes it as
  `expected_commit`, which is an **assertion** (`PIN_MOVED` if the pin has moved)
  and never a redirection of the derivation.

  For every obligation any checkpoint of that authoritatively-loaded registry
  declares, resolve the **owning work item's** implementation-stage technical
  approval **through its durable `Workflow-Technical-Approval` commit** (revision
  62, `GPT-R79-001` — the nine-step chain above, never the live record alone),
  derive the approved verifier identity from that committed record's manifest as
  an execution-complete dependency closure, resolve the bound
  conformance and derive a verdict, classified as: `PASS` (the approved
  verifier, materialized from its approved blobs and executed in isolation
  against `C`, succeeded), `FAIL` (it executed and failed, with the failing
  assertions named), `DIVERGED` (the working tree is not the pinned identity —
  see below), `PIN_MOVED` (a caller-asserted pin is no longer `HEAD`),
  `VERIFIER_UNAPPROVED` (no durable, reachable, unambiguous technical-approval
  commit authorizes the pinned content and the complete verifier closure —
  revision 61, `GPT-R78-001`; re-sourced from the approval commit, revision 62,
  `GPT-R79-001`), `VERIFIER_UNRESOLVABLE` (that authority could not be evaluated
  at all — revision 61; extended to unfollowable dynamic imports, revision 62),
  `UNKNOWN_OBLIGATION` (the registry
  declares an obligation no conformance is bound to), or `UNRESOLVABLE` (no
  commit, or a Git object read failed). **Only `PASS` satisfies**, and
  `UNKNOWN_OBLIGATION` is the fail-closed direction revision 59's (h) already
  demanded: an obligation with no executable conformance blocks completion
  permanently rather than defaulting to satisfied. A consequence worth
  stating: because the registry is loaded through the plan-approval coverage
  check, **declaring an obligation and reading it back both require the
  registry bytes to be the approved ones**, so an obligation cannot be added,
  removed, or made to disappear by an unapproved registry edit.
- `completion_obligations_satisfied(repo_root, work_item) ->
  tuple[bool, list[str]]` — `True`
  only when **every** declared obligation derives `PASS`; otherwise `False`
  plus the outstanding obligation ids and their classifications. Same
  no-caller-supplied-inputs rule. **A work item declaring no obligation returns
  `(True, [])` without resolving any approval** (revision 61, stress pass 3):
  the verifier-authority requirement attaches to obligations, never to work
  items, so an item that declares none — every legacy import, every product
  milestone — is unaffected by it.
- `work_item_completion_status(repo_root, work_item) ->
  tuple[bool, str | None, list[str]]` — the single authoritative
  terminal predicate: terminal **iff** the registry status is terminal
  **and** every completion obligation derives `PASS`. It composes the two
  existing authoritative resolvers rather than re-deriving either. It performs
  no locking of its own — it is called *by* the terminal transition while that
  transition already holds `WORKFLOW_STATE.lock`, and the conformance it runs
  is asserted never to touch the live state file or the live lock, so it cannot
  deadlock against its own caller (verified with the live lock actually held).

**The installed content must *be* the pinned identity, or the gate refuses.**
Before deriving, the gate asserts that every path on a declared writer surface
is byte-identical between the working tree and `C`, and that no untracked file
exists on a surface; any difference classifies `DIVERGED`. This is a
**precondition, not a race fix**: it can only ever cause a refusal, because the
derivation itself cannot see the working tree at all. Its purpose is to keep
"the content that was validated" and "the content that is installed" the same
thing at evaluation time, and it is what makes an *uncommitted* thirteenth
writer refuse rather than hide. The authoritative binding remains `C` in every
case.

**Which existing helper changes, and which deliberately does not.**
`select_next_checkpoint(...)` and `registry_completion_status(...)` stay
registry-only and keep their exact current semantics. That is deliberate:
`scoped_remediation_gate_reachable`/`milestone_complete_gate_reachable` split on
`is_terminal` and are documented as mutually exclusive, and continued-scope
remediation is precisely the right path while an obligation is outstanding, so
`registry_completion_status` must keep answering the checkpoint question it
answers today. `GPT-R76-003`'s required correction (3) is satisfied the other
way it allows: the higher-level completion gate explicitly rejects a terminal
registry result when an obligation is unmet.

**The gate is evaluated inside the same critical section that publishes the
transition** (new, revision 59, stress pass 3). Every transition helper in
`scripts/workflow_state.py`, `complete_work_item` included, is a pure
`state -> new_state` function whose result the *calling command* persists; the
gate therefore runs in the helper while the publication happens in the caller.
Under `D1`'s new `flock` contract that would put the gate's reads outside the
critical section and the write inside it — precisely the "locks only around the
final write while performing its read outside" shape `GPT-R76-002` forbids for
ordinary writers, and precisely the "an earlier verification step exists" fallacy
`GPT-R76-001` forbids for guarded mutations. Applying this revision's own rule
consistently: **the obligation evaluation, the registry completion resolution,
and the state publication are one critical section.** The terminal-transition
sequence is therefore `flock(LOCK_EX)` → re-read state → evaluate
`work_item_completion_status(...)` → apply `complete_work_item(...)` → canonical
serialize → publish → release.

**What that lock does and does not establish, corrected** (revision 60,
`GPT-R77-003`). Revision 59's item 356(i) claimed this ordering made evidence
mutation between gate and publish unable to produce a refused completion.
`GPT-R77-003` correctly found that `WORKFLOW_STATE.lock` serializes writers of
`WORKFLOW_STATE.json` and nothing else, and the finding was reproduced with real
processes before being accepted: with the completion process holding the lock
across evaluate-then-publish, a second process changed the evidence `PASS →
FAILED`, deleted it outright, and separately rewrote a writer's content — all
three landed unimpeded, and all three ended in `MILESTONE_COMPLETE` published
from a verdict that no longer held. The lock did its job perfectly; it simply
had no relationship to the files the verdict depended on. **That claim is
withdrawn**, and this plan does not assert that the state-file lock protects any
file it does not lock.

What replaces it is not a second re-read before publishing — `GPT-R77-003`
explicitly rules that out, and correctly: another check immediately before use
is another, smaller check/use window. What replaces it is the immutability of
the subject. Because the derivation reads only Git objects at `C`, **there is no
interval during which the verdict can change**, so there is no window to close.
The single-critical-section ordering above is retained for the reason it was
always right — the registry read and the state read must not straddle the
publish — not as a claim about evidence. Re-verified directly: with the
derivation pinned to `C`, rewriting the helper, deleting a writer, and planting
an evidence-shaped file in the working tree each left the derived verdict and
its identity bit-for-bit unchanged, while a *fresh* resolve refused the
divergence.

**The terminal transition records what authorized it — subject *and* verifier**
(revision 60, `GPT-R77-003`'s required correction (3); extended to the verifier,
revision 61, `GPT-R78-001`'s required corrections (5)/(6); extended to the
durable approval commit and the complete closure, revision 62, `GPT-R79-001`
required correction (8)/`GPT-R79-002` required correction (6)).
`complete_work_item(...)` writes into
the work item entry it returns a `completion_obligations_accepted` map — for
each obligation, the derived verdict, the **subject identity**
(`source_commit`, `obligation_content_id`), the **verifier identity**
(`verifier_identity_id`, the declared `verifier_entry`/`verifier_source_root`,
and the complete ordered `{path, mode, blob, source}` `verifier_census`), the
technical-approval provenance that authorized that verifier — **the durable
approval commit's own SHA (`technical_approval_commit`), not merely the record's
`reviewed_content_commit`** (revision 62: recording only the latter would record
what was reviewed and not *which approval event* authorized it, and the two are
different commits — the approval commit is the metadata-only commit carrying the
trailer, its `reviewed_content_commit` is the content commit it approves) —
alongside `reviewed_content_commit`, `approved_review_content_id` and the
`base_commit` the identity was recomputed over, and the discovered writer count
— published atomically with `MILESTONE_COMPLETE`
inside the same `flock` section, in the same bytes, by the same `os.replace`.

That record is exactly what a later replay needs, and the requirement is that
replay be **executable, not descriptive**. Post-completion audit can answer
"which exact `WFO-STATE-SERIALIZATION` result, implementation identity, *checker*
and *approval event* authorized this terminal transition" from the state file
alone, and can **replay** it: replay recovers the complete recorded
`verifier_census` from immutable Git objects, materializes it into an isolated
scratch tree preserving import layout, executes it in a fresh interpreter with
the live repository removed from module lookup, runs it against the recorded
immutable `source_commit`, and reproduces the recorded `obligation_content_id`
and verdict exactly. It never imports today's `workflow_state.py`,
`workflow_fingerprint.py`, or any other later repository-local code. That is
deliberately **not** "call the current `derive_obligation_verdict` with the
recorded commit" — verified across the full stress set: after later history
rewrote **both** live verifier modules to raise on import, added three unrelated
commits, and then **deleted both modules from the tree entirely**, replay from
the recorded census stayed bit-for-bit identical, and a planted `git replace`
ref over a recorded blob was refused by the `--no-replace-objects` hardening
while the same read *without* it was confirmed laundered. A recorded
`verifier_census` blob that is genuinely no longer reachable classifies
`REPLAY_UNRESOLVABLE` and refuses; replay never falls back to whatever is
running now.

The verifier identity deliberately binds the **verifier census only**, not the
whole `approved_review_content_id` (revision 61, stress pass 1). Folding the
approval digest into it was reproduced rotating the "verifier" identity whenever
a *writer* changed — re-merging the two identities this correction exists to
separate, and making a stable historical verifier identity impossible. The
approval provenance is recorded *alongside* the verifier identity, not inside
it.

**Lock ordering is fixed and single-directional** (revision 59). Two distinct
primitives now exist: the transaction mutation/handoff guard
(`PLAN_APPROVAL_MUTATION.lease`, link-based) and the state-file serialization
lock (`WORKFLOW_STATE.lock`, `flock`). Where both are held —
`D-Approval-Commits` step 8b is the only such place — the order is **guard
first, then `flock`**, released in reverse. No path anywhere takes the `flock`
before the guard, so a lock-order inversion is unreachable by construction
rather than by convention.

**The complete global partial order, in one place** (new, revision 75,
`OPUS-R92-004`; **corrected from four primitives to six and from a forest to a
DAG, revision 76, `OPUS-R93-002`**; **corrected from six primitives/four edges
to seven primitives/five edges, revision 91, self-discovered,
`WF8C-S372H-001`**; **corrected from seven primitives/five edges to eight
primitives/six edges, and two edges corrected in direction, revision 93,
external plan review, `OPUS-R117-001`/`-007`**; **corrected from eight
primitives/six edges to eight primitives/eight edges, with every edge now
classified blocking or non-blocking by its own target's primitive kind and
the acyclicity obligation restated over the blocking edges alone, revision
94, external plan review, `OPUS-R118-001`/`-002`**; **corrected from eight
primitives/eight edges to eight primitives/ten edges, with `(8)→(2)` and
`(8)→(3)` admitted and the raw edge set's own conformance evidence now
mechanically derived, in part, from the live code rather than stated only
in prose, revision 95, external plan review, `OPUS-R119-001`**). Through revision 74 the order was checkable
only by assembling three sections, and each section asserted completeness
against its own local subset — which is how the identity-gap leaf came to claim
a stated ordering while omitting `WORKFLOW_STATE.lock`. Revision 75 created this
single site and **repeated the same class of error at it**, enumerating four
primitives while this design defines six: it omitted both objects
`D-Checkpoint-Ownership` owns, each of which is defined in this same document
and each of which is exercised by the green stress passes today. That is the
second consecutive round in which a completeness claim about lock ordering was
found short — and, per `WF8C-S372H-001`, a **third**: revision 76's own
six-primitive list itself omitted `PLAN_APPROVAL_MUTATION.guardlock`, live
since `eab14ec` (item (g) part 2) and never folded back into this site, which
is why the completeness arm below is rebuilt to derive its universe from the
implementation rather than from this document's own prose (see item 372(h)
and "Revision 91" below) — a hand-maintained enumeration is, demonstrably now
three times over, the thing that goes stale, which is why the closing rule
below is a conformance obligation with a test owner rather than a convention.
This design has **eight** lock-shaped primitives:

1. the per-work-item **transaction** mutation/handoff guard
   (`.ai-review/runtime/PLAN_APPROVAL_MUTATION.lease`, link-based,
   `D-Approval-Commits`);
2. `D1`'s state-writer `flock` at `.ai-review/runtime/WORKFLOW_STATE.lock`;
3. the per-worktree identity `flock` at
   `.ai-review/runtime/WORKTREE_IDENTITY.lock` (`D-Checkpoint-Ownership`'s
   identity-document lock);
4. the repository-level identity-gap `flock` leaf at
   `$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)/ai-workflow/identity-gap.lock`;
5. the per-work-item **checkpoint** mutation/handoff guard at
   `…/checkpoint-claims/<sha256(work_item_id)>.lease` (link-based,
   `D-Checkpoint-Ownership`'s "Fencing: the mutation/handoff guard"). This is
   **not** (1): different directory, different scope, different lifecycle,
   different reclamation rules, different owning section. They are named alike
   because they are the same *primitive family*, which is exactly why omitting
   one while listing the other was easy to do and is worth naming here;
6. the guard-mutation `flock` at
   `…/checkpoint-claims/<sha256(work_item_id)>.guardlock` — stable,
   never-unlinked, carrying no ownership at rest, held for a handful of
   syscalls so that removing (5) is atomic with respect to the comparison that
   authorized the removal, **and, since revision 94 (`OPUS-R118-001`), also
   bracketing the one other create-or-remove instant this same guardlock
   protects**: `adopt_claim` (`scripts/workflow_state.py:3972`) opens this
   same `flock` to publish (8) through the identical compare-and-refuse
   `os.link` protocol, on the adoption path rather than the ordinary
   fresh-claim path — two distinct objects it can bracket depending on the
   caller, never both in the same acquisition;
7. the guard-mutation `flock` at
   `.ai-review/runtime/PLAN_APPROVAL_MUTATION.guardlock` (added, revision 91,
   self-discovered, `WF8C-S372H-001`) — (1)'s own counterpart to (6): stable,
   never-unlinked, carrying no ownership at rest, held for a handful of
   syscalls so that removing (1) is atomic with respect to the comparison
   that authorized the removal. Live since `eab14ec`
   (`acquire_plan_approval_guard`/`release_plan_approval_guard` both wrap
   their whole body in `_plan_approval_guard_lock`, structurally mirroring
   (6)'s `guard_mutation_lock` deliberately, per that commit's own message),
   never listed here until now;
8. the checkpoint claim record itself,
   `…/checkpoint-claims/<sha256(work_item_id)>.json` (link-based, admitted,
   revision 93, external plan review, `OPUS-R117-001`) — the durable record
   of who currently owns the work item and at which checkpoint, published by
   `claim_checkpoint`/`_claim_or_refuse` and removed by `release_checkpoint`'s
   compare-and-delete on `owner_token` (`assert_claim_owner`, reached inside
   guard (5)'s held interval). Through revision 92 this document excluded it
   on a per-site test — "comparing no identifier this object's own `os.link`
   protocol records" — that item 372(h)'s own general membership predicate,
   applied mechanically rather than asserted in prose, does not contain and
   that is false of the code: see item 372(h) for the full derivation and
   `WF8C-S372H-001`'s reconciliation entry for why the design intuition behind
   the old exclusion (this pathname is protected *content*, not primarily a
   mutex) is not disturbed by admitting it as a lock-order primitive too — the
   two are not exclusive, and the ordering obligation this section exists to
   close applies to every object meeting the stated predicate regardless of
   what else the object also is.

The whole order over them is **eleven edges — six blocking and five
non-blocking, widened from ten/six/four this round (workflow-v2.4.0,
plan-amendment-mechanism round 8 external implementation review,
`XMODEL-R8-B1`)** — and it is a **DAG rather than a
forest** over its blocking half; the raw eleven-edge relation itself contains
two real two-cycles and is not, and does not need to be, acyclic as a whole
(see "Blocking vs. non-blocking edges" below) — revision 75's "forest with one
edge" was a consequence of the two missing primitives, not an independent
claim:

```text
(7) PLAN_APPROVAL_MUTATION.guardlock  →  (1) PLAN_APPROVAL_MUTATION.lease  [acquire's publish, and the release's compare-and-delete]                     -- non-blocking
(1) PLAN_APPROVAL_MUTATION.lease  →  (2) WORKFLOW_STATE.lock      [D-Approval-Commits step 8b]                                                            -- blocking
(6) …/<wi>.guardlock              →  (5) checkpoint-claims/<wi>.lease  [acquire's publish, and the release's compare-and-delete]                          -- non-blocking
(6) …/<wi>.guardlock              →  (8) checkpoint-claims/<wi>.json   [adopt_claim:3972, guard held across _claim_or_refuse's os.link]                   -- non-blocking  [new, revision 94, `OPUS-R118-001`]
(5) checkpoint-claims/<wi>.lease  →  (2) WORKFLOW_STATE.lock      [steps 1d and 1f state writes]                                                           -- blocking
(5) checkpoint-claims/<wi>.lease  →  (3) WORKTREE_IDENTITY.lock   [step 1d's write_worktree_identity]                                                      -- blocking
(8) checkpoint-claims/<wi>.json   →  (5) checkpoint-claims/<wi>.lease  [steps 1d and 1f, both nested inside (8)'s own longer window]                       -- non-blocking
(8) checkpoint-claims/<wi>.json   →  (6) …/<wi>.guardlock  [owner_mutation → acquire_guard, step 1d/1f, claim held across the guardlock's real flock acquisition]  -- blocking  [new, revision 94, `OPUS-R118-002`]
(8) checkpoint-claims/<wi>.json   →  (2) WORKFLOW_STATE.lock  [step 1d: (8) published by claim_checkpoint before owner_mutation opens; the state write inside that window is reached while (8) is still held; repeated at step 1f]  -- blocking  [new, revision 95, `OPUS-R119-001`]
(8) checkpoint-claims/<wi>.json   →  (3) WORKTREE_IDENTITY.lock  [step 1d: the identity refresh inside owner_mutation's window is reached while (8) is still held]  -- blocking  [new, revision 95, `OPUS-R119-001`]
(2) WORKFLOW_STATE.lock           →  (8) checkpoint-claims/<wi>.json   [claim_checkpoint's own pre-publication phase check, XMODEL-R8-B1: publication now runs inside `state_lock`, closing the window in which a checkpoint claim could be published between `request_plan_amendment`'s authoritative `resolve_claim(...)` read and its `AMENDING_PLAN` commit -- within one worktree root only; `XMODEL-R9-B1`/`docs/defects/v2.4.0-002-amendment-claim-race-crosses-worktree-boundary.md` records that a claim published from a different linked worktree is not caught]  -- non-blocking  [new, workflow-v2.4.0 plan-amendment-mechanism round 8, `XMODEL-R8-B1`]
(4) identity-gap.lock                                             [isolated leaf, no edge either way]
```

**Not all eleven edges are code-derivable from `scripts/workflow_state.py`
alone, and this document no longer states one equality rule that silently
requires both** (revision 95, `OPUS-R119-001`, resolving the reviewer's own
`(1)→(2)` observation by generalizing it rather than leaving it a one-off
exception). Seven of the eleven — `(7)→(1)`, `(6)→(5)`, `(6)→(8)`, `(8)→(6)`,
`(8)→(5)`, `(5)→(3)`, `(2)→(8)` — are provable purely from this module's own
AST, by two structural shapes (a nested acquisition inside a guard's own
lexical `with`-block — the shape `(2)→(8)` is itself an instance of,
`claim_checkpoint`'s own body now running entirely inside a
`with state_lock(repo_root):` block, `XMODEL-R8-B1`, workflow-v2.4.0
plan-amendment-mechanism round 8; or, for primitive (8), a function that both
reaches a nested acquisition and later, in that same body, unlinks (8)'s own
pathname, proving it was already held), and are mechanically rediscovered,
bidirectionally, by a new standalone reproduction,
`docs/ai-workflow/dry-run/verify_372h_raw_edge_derivation.py`. The other
four — `(1)→(2)`, `(5)→(2)`, `(8)→(2)`, `(8)→(3)` — depend on
`.claude/commands/milestone-implement.md`'s own step ordering (which
independently callable functions this module exposes get invoked next to
each other), not on anything `scripts/workflow_state.py` itself enforces;
`(1)→(2)` additionally has no production call site at all. These four are
declared, cited to their command-file/design-intent evidence, and compared
only as a literal set against this section's own eleven-edge table — never
claimed to pass the mechanical check the other seven do. See item 372(h)'s
graph arm for the full two-tier statement of this distinction.

Read `X → Y` as "X may be held while Y is acquired". Every edge is released in
reverse acquisition order.

**Blocking vs. non-blocking edges** (new, revision 94, `OPUS-R118-001`/
`-002`): the three `os.link`-based publication entry points this design
uses — `_publish_plan_approval_guard` → (1), `_publish_guard` → (5),
`_claim_or_refuse` → (8) (corrected in place, revision 96, external plan
review, `OPUS-R120-004`: revision 95's own correction still enumerated
`_publish_claim_exclusive` as one of the three named entities in place of
the actual third entry point, `_claim_or_refuse` — the shared *statement*
`_publish_guard` and `_claim_or_refuse` both call is not itself an entry
point; `REVIEW_REQUEST.md`'s own revision-95 narrative already described
the correct three-entry-point list this sentence now carries, so the two
disagreed) — the latter two of which share one underlying `os.link`
statement, `_publish_claim_exclusive` (its two callers pass distinct
pathnames, making it one statement acquiring two primitives; attributed
caller-aware rather than over-approximated by the graph arm's own
discovery pass, revision 96, `OPUS-R120-001`, see the code-derivable tier
below), never make a concurrent acquirer wait — each one either succeeds
immediately
or fails immediately with `EEXIST`, by construction (`D-Checkpoint-Ownership`:
"no retry loop, no timeout, no wall clock"). Only `fcntl.flock` — primitives
(2), (3), (4), (6), (7) — can make a second acquirer block. So an edge
`X → Y` is a genuine deadlock hazard, one possible leg of a real circular
wait, only when `Y` is one of those five; an edge landing on `(1)`, `(5)`, or
`(8)` never is, whatever else nests inside it or nests it — `(2)→(8)`
(`XMODEL-R8-B1`, workflow-v2.4.0 plan-amendment-mechanism round 8) lands on
`(8)`, so it is non-blocking on the identical footing, regardless of `(2)`
being one of the five blocking primitives itself: the discriminator classifies
by the *target*, never the source. Of the eleven edges
above, the **blocking** ones are `(1)→(2)`, `(5)→(2)`, `(8)→(2)`, `(5)→(3)`,
`(8)→(3)`, `(8)→(6)`; the **non-blocking** ones are `(7)→(1)`, `(6)→(5)`,
`(6)→(8)`, `(8)→(5)`, `(2)→(8)`.

**The discriminator's own limit, and the one normative clause that closes
it** (added, revision 95, external plan review, `OPUS-R119-004`): the rule
above classifies by the discovery pass's `flock`/`link` *syscall tag*, not
directly by acquisition semantics — demonstrated, not hypothesized: mutating
`_publish_guard` into a genuine spin-wait retry loop around the identical
`os.link` call (`while True: try: os.link(...); break; except
FileExistsError: time.sleep(0.05)`) leaves the tag, and therefore the
classification, unchanged, even though the acquisition would then genuinely
block. The premise that makes the tag safe today — "every `os.link`
acquisition in this module is exactly one attempt: no retry loop, no
timeout, no wall clock" (`D-Checkpoint-Ownership`) — is real and is checked
by exhaustion above ("Can any `os.link` acquisition wait, retry, spin, or
sleep?"), but was not, until revision 95, bound to the discriminator
itself. **An `os.link` acquisition counts as non-blocking only if neither
its own call site, nor any frame on its static call chain, is lexically
enclosed in a loop, a `time.sleep`, or any other wait/retry construct; the
graph arm's discovery pass fails closed, naming the site, if one is found
enclosing an `os.link` acquisition it is about to classify non-blocking**
(tightened, revision 96, external plan review, `OPUS-R120-003`: revision
95's own wording scoped the check to the acquisition's own call site only,
one frame narrower than the item's own `EEXIST`-attribution rule two
paragraphs above — `OPUS-R117-002`'s "a two-frame wrapper around an
`os.link` call defeated a one-level-only climb" applies identically here: a
retry loop wrapping a *caller's* invocation of `_publish_guard`/
`_claim_or_refuse`/`_publish_plan_approval_guard`, one frame away from the
`os.link` statement itself, would satisfy a call-site-only lexical check
while genuinely introducing a wait). This is the same unbounded, transitive
climb the `EEXIST` clause already uses — one predicate over the same AST
the completeness arm already walks, mechanized in
`docs/ai-workflow/dry-run/verify_372h_raw_edge_derivation.py`'s
`enclosed_in_wait_construct` (revision 96), which mirrors that script's own
`eexist_guarded` climb through `callers_of`, substituting "encloses the
call in a `for`/`while`" for "encloses the call in a guarding `try`/
`except`" — not a new discovery mechanism, and it converts the
discriminator from "trust the syscall tag" to "derived from acquisition
semantics, with the tag as a cheap first cut," which is what this arm
already claims for itself elsewhere. On the code as it stands today this
changes no classification (no `os.link` site is so enclosed at any frame,
confirmed by the same exhaustive sweep above and reproduced by the
mechanized sweep) — the clause exists so a future wrapper cannot silently
invalidate the model by reusing the `link` tag underneath real wait
semantics one frame away from the acquisition. **Required regression check**
(new, revision 96, `OPUS-R120-003`): run
`verify_372h_raw_edge_derivation.py` against a copy of the source with
`_publish_guard`'s own call to `_publish_claim_exclusive` wrapped in a
retry loop (`while True: try: _publish_claim_exclusive(...); return; except
FileExistsError: time.sleep(0.05)`), one frame away from the `os.link`
statement itself, which stays exactly where it is, and confirm the
call-chain-aware sweep detects the enclosure — proving the check is not
merely call-site-only, the exact non-vacuousness gap this round closes.

**No back-edge exists among the blocking edges, and none may be introduced**
— restated from the revision-75-through-93 blanket form, which the real
`(6)↔(8)` pair (below) falsifies as a claim about the raw relation; in
particular **(2) is never held while (5) is acquired**, which remains
prohibited by design — a state writer that wants to fence a checkpoint
transition it is about to record is the natural way to write it, and it
would break the ownership/authority separation `D-Checkpoint-Ownership`
depends on regardless of its own blocking classification, so this specific
inversion stays forbidden unconditionally, not only because of the
deadlock-freedom argument above. The `(6)`/`(8)` pair, both directions
already declared and evidenced below, was through revision 99 the **sole**
pre-approved exception to raw-graph antisymmetry; the `(2)`/`(8)` pair is now
a **second** (workflow-v2.4.0, plan-amendment-mechanism round 8,
`XMODEL-R8-B1`: `(8)→(2)` already existed, from step 1d/1f's own
`claim_checkpoint`-then-`owner_mutation` command-file sequencing; `(2)→(8)`
is the new, opposite-direction, genuinely nested edge `claim_checkpoint`'s own
`state_lock`-guarded pre-publication phase check adds) — no other pair may
acquire a second, opposite-direction edge without this section being updated
first. **Two edges
corrected in direction, revision 93, external plan review, `OPUS-R117-007`**
(applied per explicit user direction; the reviewer's own disposition was
"recorded only, no change requested" — see item 372(h)'s "Direction semantics
of every edge" for the full derivation): revision 91's `(1)→(7)` and revision
76's `(5)→(6)` both read the lease as the long-lived container relative to
its own guardlock, which is the lease's role everywhere *else* in this graph
but not here — `acquire_plan_approval_guard`/`acquire_guard`
open the guardlock first and publish the lease inside that window (ordinary
path and reclaim branch alike), and `release_plan_approval_guard`/`release_guard`
open the guardlock first and remove the lease inside that same window, so the
guardlock's own critical section is the one that is open in both directions,
never the lease's.

Four per-primitive properties, extended to five (corrected from "Two", stale
since revision 76 added the third without updating the count, revision 91;
extended for the corrected (6)/(7) direction and the new (8), revision 93,
external plan review, `OPUS-R117-001`/`-007`; (6)'s and (8)'s degrees
corrected again, revision 94, external plan review, `OPUS-R118-001`/`-002`),
stated at the strength each mechanism actually has:

- **(3) is a leaf in one direction only**, which is how
  `D-Checkpoint-Ownership`'s own defining bullet states it and how it is
  restated here: *no other lock in this design is ever acquired while (3) is
  held*. It **is** acquired while (5) is held — step 1d's guarded mutation is
  `transition_checkpoint_in_progress` **plus `write_worktree_identity`**, and
  the latter takes (3) for its whole load → validate → mutate → publish
  sequence. Revision 75 strengthened this to a two-directional leaf claim
  ("neither is ever acquired while another is held"), which the mechanism does
  not satisfy and never did. Nothing about the mechanism changes here; the claim
  is brought back to it.
- **(4) is the only genuine isolated leaf**, and its rule stays concrete rather
  than asserted: its hold interval ends at "admit", strictly before the
  `WORKFLOW_STATE.json` write that follows, and the identity query's read of the
  durable authorization record takes no lock at all, so a query evaluated inside
  (2) acquires nothing.
- **(7) is a root; (6) is not** (corrected in place, revision 94,
  `OPUS-R118-001`/`-002`; through revision 93 both were stated as roots with
  exactly one out-edge each — `(7)` still is, on both counts, `(6)` is not,
  on either). `(7)`: nothing is ever held when it is acquired, and it has
  exactly one edge, out, to the lease it exists solely to bracket, `(7)→(1)`.
  Its critical section touches only that lease, in both the acquire path
  (publish, or reclaim-and-republish) and the release path
  (compare-and-delete), and always closes — releasing `(7)` — before `(1)`
  goes on, separately and later, to nest `(2)`. `(6)`: it now has **two**
  out-edges, `(6)→(5)` (unchanged) and `(6)→(8)` (`adopt_claim`, publishing
  an adopted claim through the same compare-and-refuse protocol as `(5)`),
  and **one** in-edge, `(8)→(6)` (`owner_mutation`'s `acquire_guard`, reached
  from `release_checkpoint` at step 1f and from step 1d's checkpoint
  transition, opens `(6)` while `(8)` is durably published and not yet
  removed) — so `(6)` is neither a root nor "exactly one edge, out" any
  longer. Both of `(6)`'s own out-edges stay non-blocking — `(5)` and `(8)`
  are both `os.link`-based, so neither acquisition can ever make `(6)`'s
  holder wait — and `(6)`'s critical section still always closes, on every
  path, before the object it just touched (`(5)` or `(8)`) goes on,
  separately and later, to nest anything else: `(6)→(5)→(2)`,
  `(6)→(5)→(3)`, and `(6)→(8)→(6)` are real paths in the raw graph, not real
  overlaps in execution — the last one is not a cycle in the property that
  matters; see "Blocking vs. non-blocking edges" above. Neither `(6)` nor
  `(7)` is ever held simultaneously with (2), and neither reaches (2)
  transitively through any blocking path.
- **(8) has four out-edges and two in-edges, none reached only through (5)**
  (in-edge count corrected in place, workflow-v2.4.0 plan-amendment-mechanism
  round 8, `XMODEL-R8-B1`, for the new `(2)→(8)` -- see below; out-edge count
  corrected in place, revision 95, `OPUS-R119-002`: through revision 94 the
  heading itself said "one out-edge and one in-edge," contradicted by this
  same bullet's own body three sentences later, "`(8)` therefore contributes

  through revision 93 stated as "a leaf reached from (5) only", which relied
  on `(5)→(6)` — a direction revision 93 itself had already reversed to
  `(6)→(5)` before that bullet was written, so `(6)` was never actually

  `<checkpoint-claims>/<sha256(work_item_id)>.json` is created, unguarded, by

  `adopt_claim` under (6) (the adoption path), and is not removed until

  and 1f), and across step 1d's own `claim_checkpoint`-then-`owner_mutation`

  both of those `owner_mutation` windows nest a fresh `(5)` acquisition

  `(8)→(2)`/`(8)→(3)` (new, revision 95, `OPUS-R119-001`): at step 1d, `(8)`

  reopen the acyclicity obligation. The other three out-edges, `(8)→(5)`,
  `(8)→(2)`, `(8)→(3)`, are new only in the sense that this bullet now states

  "held in the outstanding-existence sense" argument already established for
  the first of the three. `(2)→(8)` (new, workflow-v2.4.0 plan-amendment-mechanism round 8, external

  `with state_lock(...):` block, so `(2)` is genuinely held while `(8)` is
  acquired — the mirror image of `(8)→(2)`'s own "held in the
  outstanding-existence sense" fact above, which remains true and unaffected

  about a *nested* acquisition of `(8)` inside `(2)`'s own momentary

  flow, never open at once). This closes `XMODEL-R8-B1`: before this round, a
  checkpoint claim could still be published, unguarded by anything in the
  `WORKFLOW_STATE.json` domain, in the exact window between
  `request_plan_amendment`'s own authoritative `resolve_claim(...)` read

  took `(2)` at all. Sharing `(2)` between the two operations makes them
  strictly ordered: whichever acquires `(2)` first completes its entire
  critical section — either `claim_checkpoint`'s own phase check and
  publication, or `request_plan_amendment`'s entire supersede-and-commit —
  before the other's begins, so a claim can never be published into an
  amendment's own quiescence window, and `request_plan_amendment`'s

  published after it ran but before `AMENDING_PLAN` was durable --
  **within one worktree root.** `(2)` (`WORKFLOW_STATE.lock`) resolves as

  worktree*, while `(8)`'s own home `claims_dir(repo_root)` is

  repository -- so this closure does not extend to an amendment requested
  in one linked worktree racing a checkpoint claim published from another
  (`XMODEL-R9-B1`, round 9 external implementation review). A second,
  independent reason it cannot: `claim_checkpoint`'s own phase check reads
  `repo_root / DEFAULT_STATE_PATH`, that worktree's own working-tree copy
  of `WORKFLOW_STATE.json`, which cannot observe a phase committed only to
  another worktree's own branch, however well the two operations are
  serialized. This release deliberately leaves that residual open rather
  than half-fixing it -- see
  `docs/defects/v2.4.0-002-amendment-claim-race-crosses-worktree-boundary.md`
  for the full accounting and what a real fix would need.

**The blocking edges are acyclic, and that is the property deadlock-freedom
actually requires; the raw eleven-edge graph is not acyclic, and does not need
to be** (restated, revision 95, `OPUS-R119-001`, widening revision 94's
identical four-edge argument to six edges without changing its shape;
revision 94, `OPUS-R118-001`/`-002`, had itself replaced the
revision-75-through-93 blanket acyclicity claim, which the real `(6)→(8)`/
`(8)→(6)` pair falsifies as a claim about the raw relation; the blocking
sub-order itself is unwidened by workflow-v2.4.0 round 8's own new edge,
`(2)→(8)`, since it is non-blocking): the blocking
edges are `(1)→(2)`, `(5)→(2)`, `(8)→(2)`, `(5)→(3)`, `(8)→(3)`, `(8)→(6)`
(see "Blocking vs. non-blocking edges" above for why these six, and only
these six, are the ones a real circular wait could ever be built from).
Their sources are `(1)`, `(5)`, `(8)` — unchanged by this revision, since
`(8)`'s two new blocking edges share the same source `(8)` already had —
their targets are `(2)`, `(3)`, `(6)` — likewise unchanged, since `(8)→(2)`
and `(8)→(3)` land on targets `(5)→(2)`/`(5)→(3)` already declared; and none
of `(2)`, `(3)`, `(6)` has an outgoing blocking edge — `(6)`'s own two
out-edges, `(6)→(5)` and `(6)→(8)`, are both non-blocking — so no blocking
edge ever chains into another and no cycle is constructible among them. This
was checked the same way revision 94 checked the eight-edge graph: takeover,
abandoned destructive-guard recovery, `authorize_identity_reference_gap`,
identity establishment, state mutation and the bootstrap transaction were
each traced again against the corrected eleven-edge, blocking/non-blocking-
classified graph, and no blocking cycle is constructible in any of them.

The raw graph — blocking and non-blocking edges together, "X may be held
while Y is acquired," with no distinction drawn — **does** contain two cycles:
`(6)→(8)` (`adopt_claim`, non-blocking) and `(8)→(6)` (`owner_mutation` →
`acquire_guard`, blocking) both hold, both are real, live code, and neither
is an ad-hoc exception or a rejected finding — see `OPUS-R118-001`/`-002`'s
disposition below; likewise `(2)→(8)` (`claim_checkpoint`'s own
`state_lock`-guarded publication, non-blocking) and `(8)→(2)` (`owner_mutation`'s
own later, separate state write, blocking) both hold, both real, live code,
neither an ad-hoc exception (workflow-v2.4.0 round 8, `XMODEL-R8-B1`). This is
stated plainly, once, so no future round mistakes
the raw graph's two-cycles for an oversight the checks below failed to catch:
those checks do not test the raw graph for acyclicity at all — they test the
declared **edge set** (raw, all eleven, by simple set equality — no
acyclicity requirement) and the declared **blocking sub-order** (acyclicity,
the property above) as two separate, independent assertions, exactly as item
372(h)'s graph arm now states them. So the correction here is to the
**page**, not to the mechanism — the same disposition `OPUS-R92-004`
received, and stated as plainly.

**Any future primitive — or any future *edge* between two primitives already on
this list — must be added here, with its position and its edges stated, before
it is used at any call site, and this is a conformance obligation, not a
convention** (revision 76; **extended from primitives to edges, revision 77,
`OPUS-R94-002`**). The extension is not cosmetic: the primitive half of this
rule was already enforced mechanically, while a new nested acquisition between
two listed primitives was constrained by nothing — it contradicts no recorded
edge and introduces no cycle, so it could land while leaving this site
documenting five of six real edges. Item 372(h) owns both halves: every
lock-shaped pathname satisfying the membership predicate stated there is
discovered mechanically from the live code (corrected in place, revision 92,
`OPUS-R116-003`, replacing the retired "every ... pathname this document
defines" wording that named the very prose-derived mechanism `WF8C-S372H-001`
proved structurally blind) and asserted to appear in this list, the derived
edge set is asserted **equal** to the **eleven** recorded edges (corrected in
place, revision 92, `OPUS-R116-003`, from the stale "four" left uncorrected
when revision 91 added `(1)→(7)`; corrected again, revision 93, `OPUS-R117-001`,
from five to six for the new `(8)→(5)` edge; corrected again, revision 94,
`OPUS-R118-001`/`-002`, from six to eight for `(6)→(8)` and `(8)→(6)`;
corrected again, revision 95, `OPUS-R119-001`, from eight to ten for
`(8)→(2)` and `(8)→(3)`; corrected again, workflow-v2.4.0 plan-amendment-mechanism
round 8, `XMODEL-R8-B1`, from ten to eleven for `(2)→(8)`) and names any
unrecorded one — this is now stated
as **two separate conformance obligations, not one** (revision 94): raw-set
equality over all eleven edges (no acyclicity requirement — this is the check
that would catch a hypothetical `(2)→(5)` inversion, exactly as before), and
acyclicity of the **blocking edges alone** ("Blocking vs. non-blocking
edges" above). Three live control arms are carried — an inverted `(2) →
(5)` acquisition that the raw-set equality check must name as undeclared
(still true, and, additionally, since its target `(5)` is non-blocking, not
a case the blocking-acyclicity check alone would catch — the two
obligations are independently load-bearing, which is exactly why both are
required); an extra acyclic `(1)→(3)` acquisition that the equality must
name; and a hypothetical direct `(6)→(2)` edge (bypassing (5)
entirely) — its target is blocking, so it is asserted to be caught by the
blocking-acyclicity check (it would not itself close a cycle, but
demonstrates the check inspects blocking edges by their own targets, not by
inheriting acyclicity from the raw-set check). The rule as revision 75
wrote it was already violated by two primitives in use at the moment it was
written, which is what a convention with no owner is worth.

**Seven of the eleven edges are now mechanically re-derived from the live
code, not merely asserted in prose** (added, revision 95, external plan
review, `OPUS-R119-001`, per explicit user direction: "make its conformance
evidence mechanically derive the raw edge set from the actual hold/acquire
lifetimes, analogous to the now-code-derived primitive-membership arm, so a
future extra edge fails automatically" — resolving the recurring class of
defect this section's own history already names five times over,
`OPUS-R92-004`, `OPUS-R93-002`, `WF8C-S372H-001`, `OPUS-R118-001`/`-002`,
and this finding; widened from six to seven, workflow-v2.4.0
plan-amendment-mechanism round 8, `XMODEL-R8-B1`, for `(2)→(8)`).
A new standalone reproduction,
`docs/ai-workflow/dry-run/verify_372h_raw_edge_derivation.py`, walks the
same AST the completeness arm's own script already parses and mechanically
rediscovers, bidirectionally, exactly the seven edges provable from
`scripts/workflow_state.py` alone — `(7)→(1)`, `(6)→(5)`, `(6)→(8)`,
`(8)→(6)`, `(8)→(5)`, `(5)→(3)`, `(2)→(8)` — by two structural shapes (a nested
acquisition inside a guard's own lexical `with`-block, an instance
`claim_checkpoint`'s own `with state_lock(repo_root):`-guarded publication
now is too; and, scoped specifically to primitive (8), a function that both
reaches a nested acquisition and later, in that same body, unlinks (8)'s own
pathname, proving it was already durably held). Both directions are checked: a
spurious extra edge (a synthetic nested acquisition injected into
`write_worktree_identity`'s own guard) is asserted to make the forward
check fail, naming it; a missing edge (both live call paths to `(5)→(3)`
removed) is asserted to make the reverse check fail. **The other four
declared edges are not claimed to pass this mechanical check, and this is
stated as an explicit distinction rather than left for one equality rule to
paper over** (resolving `OPUS-R119`'s own request to "resolve `(1)→(2)`
consistently"): `(1)→(2)`, `(5)→(2)`, `(8)→(2)`, `(8)→(3)` each depend on
`.claude/commands/milestone-implement.md`'s own step ordering — which
independently callable functions this module exposes get invoked next to
each other — not on anything `scripts/workflow_state.py` itself enforces
(`(1)→(2)` additionally has no production call site at all, per
`OPUS-R116-004`). These four are tracked in the script as an explicit,
separately-labeled, non-mechanical list, compared only as a literal set
against this section's own declared eleven-edge table, so a silent divergence
between the script's Tier-2 list and this document's prose still fails —
just not by re-deriving semantics the module's own AST cannot express.

**Every command that can make the work item terminal consumes it.**
- `complete_work_item(...)` — the sole writer of `MILESTONE_COMPLETE`, and
  therefore the sole path `/accept-milestone` can reach a terminal phase
  through. Its existing `IncompleteOwnCheckpointsError` gate is joined by a new
  `UnsatisfiedCompletionObligationError`, raised when
  `completion_obligations_satisfied(...)` is `False`, naming each outstanding
  obligation, its classification (`FAIL`/`DIVERGED`/`PIN_MOVED`/
  `UNKNOWN_OBLIGATION`/`UNRESOLVABLE`) and, for `FAIL`, the specific
  conformance assertions that failed. Marking
  `WF8b`'s registry checkpoint `COMPLETE` — by hand, by
  `complete_checkpoint(...)`, or by any other means — is therefore **not
  sufficient by itself**.
- `/accept-scoped-remediation` / `apply_scoped_remediation_acceptance(...)` —
  the non-terminal acceptance path. It does not and must not reach
  `MILESTONE_COMPLETE`, so it is not a bypass; the requirement is that it
  cannot *become* one, which it cannot, because `complete_work_item` remains
  the only writer of the terminal phase. This is asserted rather than assumed
  (item 356).
- Any future command that can write a terminal phase must call
  `work_item_completion_status(...)`; item 356 asserts that the set of writers
  of `MILESTONE_COMPLETE` is exactly `complete_work_item`.

**Quiescence retirement consumes the identical verdict, under identical rules —
but it belongs to the *permanent* command, not to the temporary bootstrap
bridge** (rewritten, revision 61, resolves `GPT-R78-002`). The obligation
concept is shared exactly as `GPT-R76-003`'s required correction (5) and
`GPT-R77-003`'s required correction (4) demand: whichever consumer asks, it
calls the same function, with the same no-caller-supplied-inputs rule, the same
`HEAD` pinning, the same divergence precondition, the same verifier-authority
resolution and the same fail-closed classifications, so "the window may be
retired" and "`WF8b` may complete" cannot disagree in either direction. What
revision 61 removes is the claim that the **temporary bootstrap bridge** can
perform that retirement:

- **The temporary bridge never consults the obligation.** It always requires the
  explicit current-turn user quiescence authorization, it never pins a commit,
  and it can therefore never produce `PIN_MOVED`. See `D-Approval-Commits` step
  4a and its "Temporary state-writer quiescence window" subsection, both
  rewritten this revision.
- **The permanent `/approve-review` (item 347) is the retirement point.** Once
  item 354 is implemented, its implementation independently reviewed and
  technically approved, and the derived, verifier-authorized conformance passes,
  that command may use `WFO-STATE-SERIALIZATION` in place of the temporary
  authorization.

Revision 60 wired the retirement into the bridge and `GPT-R78-002` found the
result internally inconsistent in three independent ways, all confirmed against
the authoritative text before acceptance: step 4a still required the literal
authorization unconditionally with no branch for the `PASS` case; the
schema-version-3 journal defines `quiescence_authorization` as the user's
literal text validated to name the work item and stage, with nowhere to put a
commit; and the pin was necessarily invalidated by the transaction's own
approval commit at step 6, which deterministically moves `HEAD` from `C` to `A`
before step 8b reads it back. The sentence "it carries the pinned `C` in the
journal's `quiescence_authorization` record and passes it back as
`expected_commit`" is **withdrawn**: `quiescence_authorization` carries the
literal authorization string and nothing else, and no consumer in this plan
asserts that a pre-approval `HEAD` SHA must still be `HEAD` after its own
approval commit.

**The permanent command pins identities, not `HEAD`** (revision 61, stress pass
2). It evaluates the obligation before its own mutations and pins the derived
`(obligation_content_id, verifier_identity_id)`; at the use point it re-derives
with the *same approved verifier* and requires those two identities to
reproduce. Both are invariant under the approval commit, whose exact committed
path set contains no file on a writer surface and no file in the verifier path
set — while any unrelated intervening change to either surface rotates them and
refuses. A HEAD-SHA pin cannot express that and a second approval-currency
resolution after the commit must not be used either: when the conditional fifth
member applies, the approval commit rewrites
`docs/ai-workflow/registry/workflow-v2-1-core-artifacts.json`, which is
implementation-stage protected by exact path, so re-resolving currency
afterwards would have the command stale its own authority with its own required
commit. That was reproduced, and the identity-pinning rule is what avoids it.
`expected_commit` survives as an assertion available to any caller that pins and
uses within a single un-committing window; it can only ever refuse, and the
temporary bridge does not use it.

**Cost, stated rather than hand-waved.** Deriving instead of caching means the
conformance runs at every gate evaluation. That is affordable because the gate
is evaluated rarely — `/accept-milestone`'s terminal transition and the bridge's
quiescence decision — and because the conformance is bounded: a static pass over
the discovered surface plus a fixed, small behavioural suite. Measured on this
repository's own hardware against the prototype, the whole derivation including
the behavioural sub-suite completes in well under a second. The behavioural
sub-suite spawns real processes, but always against a scratch root holding a
copy of the helper materialized from `C` — never the live state file and never
`.ai-review/runtime/WORKFLOW_STATE.lock` — which is what keeps it safe to run
from inside the terminal critical section.

**The behavioural sub-suite is deterministic, not probabilistic** (revision 60,
stress pass 3). A gate whose refusal depends on winning a race is not a gate. The
suite therefore leads with a barrier-based interleaving test: a harness holds the
lock, lets a writer start, then publishes a value and releases. A publisher that
reads *inside* the critical section necessarily observes that value and preserves
it; one that reads outside necessarily clobbers it. The N-way concurrent-writer
test is retained as an additional check, not as the discriminator. Before this
was added, the only thing separating a correct publisher from a
`read-outside-the-lock` one was whether sixteen racing processes happened to
interleave badly.

**Generality, without broadening this revision.** The mechanism is defined once
and used once. Future continued-scope obligations that are completion-blocking
declare a `WFO-` id on their owning checkpoint and register a conformance
callable against that id; nothing further is needed, and items 356/357 are
written against the mechanism rather than against `WFO-STATE-SERIALIZATION`
specifically, so a second obligation is covered the day it is declared. The
binding from obligation id to conformance lives in the implementation rather
than the registry, so it is covered by implementation-stage review while the
